However, the effectiveness of these models can be compromised in text code manipulation tasks due to their reliance on pre-encoded semantic information. We introduce a novel approach, SemAug, which enhances the semantic representation of these models through data augmentation techniques. SemAug increases the diversity of input sequences in a masked code filling task, thereby enhancing the semantic representation and its transferability to other programming tasks. The observed diversity in galaxy morphologies can be broadly categorized into disc and spheroid types. We present a study that combines data from CALIFA and SAMI to investigate the spatial distribution of stellar populations within 63 galaxies. Our analysis reveals that galaxies with a disc or spheroid morphology exhibit distinct distribution patterns of stellar populations. Furthermore, we find that spheroids are composed of multiple sub-components, each with different properties. We propose a scenario in which disc galaxies form through continuous accretion of gas, while spheroids emerge from mergers resulting in the dissipation of debris and the formation of a rotating, gas-rich precursor. Our findings also suggest that spheroids may form through the inside-out growth of a massive, gas-rich galaxy. However, further investigation is required to confirm this hypothesis. Ultimately, our results imply that galactic discs and spheroids have distinct and complex formation histories. The DWIFOB algorithm is a stable variant of the Anderson acceleration technique for
inconsistent stochastic optimization. Our research reveals that this variant generates
sequences contained within a convex polyhedral region. Building upon this finding,
we developed a robust version of the DWIFOB algorithm that provides sequential guarantees
and outperforms the robust Anderson acceleration method by several performance metrics. 
Specifically, the robust DWIFOB algorithm exhibits faster convergence and greater solution
accuracy than the robust Anderson acceleration method, particularly in the presence of noise. 
Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the superior
performance of the robust DWIFOB algorithm over the robust Anderson acceleration method. 
Interestingly, the robust DWIFOB algorithm also serves as a descent method, offering additional
benefits. To our knowledge, this is the first descent algorithm based on DWIFOB. 
Ultimately, the robust DWIFOB algorithm represents a more effective and efficient tool for
stochastic optimization.

Offline optimization tasks often rely on utility functions defined by pairwise preferences or utility functions estimated from expert knowledge. However, learning a utility function in this way is typically an underdetermined problem, forcing methods to make strong assumptions. We investigate the trade-offs between assumptions made by pairwise result preference optimization and utility function estimation from expert knowledge. We find that pairwise result preference optimization is not necessary to make assumptions and that learning a utility function from expert knowledge with fewer assumptions is possible. To achieve this, we propose a utility function learning method that estimates a utility function and expert noise parameters using only mean reward feedback. Our method is based on variational inference and can be efficiently trained offline. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by showing it outperforms pairwise result preference optimization methods that we adapted for utility function learning. Our method also generalizes well to new tasks and is more robust to incorrect expert knowledge than other methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/aryashah2k/DUET.

Reinforcement learning agents often exhibit undesirable behaviors when their training is paused or resumed. Understanding and anticipating these behaviors could lead to better methods for pause detection and agent rectification. Prior studies have primarily focused on identifying pause periods, but little attention has been given to using sequence-to-sequence models to forecast future agent actions during pauses. We introduce a novel approach that leverages these models to make pause period predictions more accurate. This method involves training an encoder-decoder network on action sequences, then using it to estimate future actions during pauses by sampling action sequences. The proposed method outperforms baseline pause period prediction methods and achieves higher accuracy when compared to simply continuing agent actions. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/kevin-kuang/Forecasting-Agent-Actions.

Furthermore, we derive from this structure the information that the chain of subgroups formed by the iterations of the map is stationary. In string theory, supersymmetry serves as a fundamental constraint ensuring that low-energy effective couplings maintain physical integrity. However, this constraint can be relaxed in the process of moduli stabilization through non-perturbative dynamics. We investigate the impact of this process in heterotic string theory on a Calabi-Yau manifold featuring enhanced symmetries. Focusing on the specific case of a quintic polynomial defining the manifold, we show that the low-energy effective couplings in the supersymmetric theory are subject to intricate relationships. These relationships are reexamined in the limit of large complex structure where the theory loses supersymmetry due to dynamical instability. By resolving the quintic as a sum of five intersecting plane polynomials, we derive new mathematical expressions for the low-energy effective couplings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the high degree terms in the couplings can be eliminated, thereby recovering the previous supersymmetry constraints. Ultimately, our findings provide a connection between the worldsheet and the physical world, offering a novel perspective on string theory. Additionally, our work may have broader implications for understanding complex geometric structures in mathematics. A comprehensive mathematical framework supporting our results is presented in the accompanying paper, titled "Fivefold Symmetry and Low-Energy Couplings" [arXiv:2205.13445]. Identifying influential users in social networks is crucial for various purposes, 
such as marketing and epidemic prevention. Previous studies have employed various 
approaches, including graph neural networks, to tackle this problem. This paper 
investigates the impact of augmentation strategies, both during training and 
evaluation, on influential user prediction in social networks. We analyzed 
multiple datasets from different sources and found that improvements gained 
initially decrease progressively as graph size increases. Notably, test-time 
augmentation is found to be more effective than train-time augmentation. We 
also discovered that utilizing a pre-trained encoder and a linear classifier 
yields better results when combined with train-time augmentation. Our findings 
provide valuable insights for selecting effective augmentation methods and 
improve current methods, leading to significant performance enhancements. We 
publicly released our code and preprocessed datasets to facilitate future 
research.

This research introduces an advanced method for pose estimation that utilizes deep learning to account for a variety of errors in sensor readings. Unlike existing approaches, which often restrict themselves to random noise, this technique develops a model that can capture more comprehensive correlations in the error process. The framework is based on a new, richly structured additive Gaussian error model that can effectively represent diverse correlations in sensor data. By formulating this model as a low-rank factorization problem, this approach can be solved efficiently using a range of optimization algorithms. The technique can be enhanced by incorporating prior knowledge of sensor relationships. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation and real-world experiments involving a mobile robot's 3D pose estimation from stereo camera images. The results show that incorporating more general correlations significantly improves estimation accuracy. Additionally, the method's ability to incorporate prior information is validated in these experiments. This hypothesis naturally arises from the superimposition of an dark matter and dark energy component in a single fluid. We investigate how such a scenario affects the evolution of the universe on various scales, specifically the cosmic microwave background, galaxy clusters, and dark matter particles. By taking into account the different temperatures, we derive a modified equation for the Hubble expansion and the Jeans mass, which in turn influences the CMB and dark matter particle interactions. Our analysis reveals that a multi-temperature universe may yield a broader range of acceptable dark matter particle cross-sections, particularly for masses between approximately 10 GeV and 10 TeV. This idea could offer a new perspective on the long-standing problem of reconciling particle physics and cosmological observations. We examine its potential implications for direct dark matter detection experiments and the LHC, as well as the observable signatures of dark matter in galaxies. Our multi-temperature universe model may be tested by future high-precision CMB experiments, such as the CMB-S4, through precise measurements of lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect. Furthermore, the multi-temperature effect can be probed through the study of the Sun's gravitational capture of dark matter particles, which could be within the reach of future direct detection experiments operating underground. Finally, the multi-temperature hypothesis may also be tested by future 21 cm experiments, such as the SKA, through precise measurements of the global signal and global polarization. We also discuss the potential limitations of our multi-temperature universe model arising from the backreaction of dark matter and dark energy on the cosmic fluid. We find that for a wide range of multi-temperature values, the backreaction does not significantly impact the evolution of the universe. However, in the limiting case where the backreaction is significant, we find that the resulting cosmological parameters may still be consistent with current observational data. We also explore the potential impact of a multi-temperature universe on primordial non-Gaussianity, which could be within the reach of future high-precision CMB experiments. Performance evaluations demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art colorization techniques in both familiar and unfamiliar object settings. This study investigates the collaborative management of shared files within groups of software developers working together in environments like Git. We analyzed maintenance habits within 12,624 repository pairs from the GitHub platform, focusing on files shared across these repositories. The results show that the way these files are managed is highly inconsistent, with each group having its unique approach to file collaboration. We also found that the likelihood of a group's files being actively maintained is linked to the presence of specific technical contributors, known as 'liason' members, who tend to handle file management. Furthermore, the study revealed that successful collaboration on shared files depends on clear naming conventions and consistent directory structures within a repository. These findings provide valuable insights for improving collaborative software development and understanding the social aspects of file management. Based on this understanding, the ROLLUP tool was developed to help groups maintain and organize their shared files more effectively. Deep neural networks are widely used for classification tasks, but they can produce unreliable outcomes due to their tendency to make predictions with high confidence levels beyond their actual scope of certainty. This can be problematic in situations where incorrect predictions with high confidence can result in adverse consequences. To mitigate this issue, we have developed a novel method called the Predictive Uncertainty Guided Adversarial Attack, which identifies and prioritizes the network's existing limitations before attempting to breach its defenses. The purpose of this method is not merely to generate aggressive attacks, but also to utilize the gained knowledge to inform the development of a new, robust model that incorporates predictive uncertainty into its training process. By integrating this new model into the training pipeline, we can prevent overfitting and produce accurate class predictions by capping the influence of unreliable features. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing the accuracy of deep learning models. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/asharif22/PUGAA.

A preprint serves as an early version of a research article that can be shared before formal peer review. Authors whose work is posted as preprints also experience increased article-level metrics and faster publication times. Notably, the benefits of preprints extend beyond authors who post multiple preprints, and even minimal preprint exposure has a positive effect. This research suggests that preprints are an effective means of accelerating research dissemination and should be utilized more widely. By doing so, researchers can capitalize on preprints' numerous benefits, including enhanced research visibility, faster publication times, and increased citation counts. A potential drawback of preprints is their potential for disseminating incorrect or flawed research. However, this risk can be mitigated through clear preprint labels and copyright statements, as well as targeted outreach efforts to specific fields. Ultimately, the advantages of preprints outweigh the disadvantages, and they hold significant promise for the scientific community. However, we find that these algorithms produce coadded images with fluctuating point spread function (PSF) profiles, particularly if star twilights have significantly different PSF shapes. This PSF instability affects the accuracy of photometry, particularly for the clipped-mean method, which can result in an error of up to 0.3 magnitudes for certain galaxy observations. In contrast, the mean combination yields the most consistent PSF, with the least impact on photometry. We provide a mathematical explanation for the PSF instability in nonlinear combinations and suggest potential workarounds to minimize this effect. Ultimately, the choice of coaddition algorithm depends on the specific requirements of the science application and the characteristics of the data being analyzed. Data augmentation is a widely used technique to enhance machine learning models. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated in various applications, but the impact on sound event detection systems is not well understood. This study investigates the benefits of data augmentation for sound event detection, specifically in the context of the DCASE 2020 challenge data. We found that data augmentation significantly improves model performance when training sets are limited, but has no discernible effect when training sets are abundant. This finding is attributed to data augmentation's ability to increase model generalizability and tolerance of minor errors. Furthermore, data augmentation's advantages are most pronounced in detecting infrequent sound events. However, the improved performance comes with the cost of heightened model-fitting errors. Consequently, data augmentation should be considered a means to enhance model robustness, but should not be relied upon to reduce fitting errors. Ultimately, data augmentation is a valuable tool that can be effectively utilized to improve sound event detection systems, particularly those with limited training data. Our research findings provide insights for future sound event detection studies. Wildfires pose a significant threat to the atmosphere, causing air quality to severely deteriorate in affected areas. Predicting the transport of aerosol optical depth (AOD) resulting from wildfires is crucial for forecasting air quality. In evolutionary studies, researchers often focus on the behavior of individual gene substitutions or new mutations.  However, for many such events, their average impact is more predictable than their individual outcome.  This paper introduces a statistical approach to analyze average effects of gene substitutions and new mutations, which offers a more manageable framework than examining their sole consequences.  It's demonstrated that this method can be applied to various evolutionary models, including Fisher's fundamental theorem and models of quantitative evolution, which involve multiple interacting genes. In the personalized semi-supervised learning (PSL) framework, a semi-supervised learning approach is implemented on a decentralized network of edge devices. These devices are equipped with a function that combines their local data and model, allowing them to make personalized assumptions about unlabeled data. After updating their local models, the devices share tailored assumptions with a central server, which incorporates them into a global model through matrix factorization. The server then redistributes the updated model and assumptions to the devices. Experimental results show that PSL leads to significant performance improvements, especially on devices with limited labeled data. In a multi-agent system, agents face choices about how to allocate time between various tasks of differing difficulties. Moreover, a decentralized controller can achieve similar outcomes by guiding agents' perception of the difficulty distribution. The study provides a theoretical framework for controlling multi-agent systems based on task difficulty distribution and validates its effectiveness through simulations. Additionally, the findings are applied to a complex problem in swarm robotics, demonstrating the potential for significant performance enhancement. Our research investigates the influence of background effects, tied to local charge conservation, on the measurement of charge-dependent correlations in high-energy collisions. Calculations based on an analytical model of the freeze-out indicate that the fourth and fifth cumulants of the WCA distribution are sensitive to background effects, with values ranging from 20% to 100% due to local charge conservation. Innovative applications of federated learning in network intrusion detection systems hold promise for significant improvements in privacy and collaboration. Semi-supervised node classification in Graph Neural Networks is enhanced by pseudo-labeling techniques that assign labels to unlabeled nodes. Current pseudo-labeling approaches, however, introduce noisy labels after node feature transformation, potentially harming large Graph Neural Networks. To address this issue, we propose an efficient method that limits pseudo-label noise by assigning labels before feature transformation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various datasets, outperforming existing pseudo-labeling methods. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/ChenXu1998/PL4GNN.  Jacobo Borda contributed equally to this work.

This paper introduces PatchNet, a lightweight and efficient neural network designed for video object detection. By breaking down feature maps into smaller, non-overlapping regions called patches, PatchNet effectively processes video data in a frame-by-frame manner. Unlike other approaches, PatchNet does not rely on explicit motion information, instead leveraging aggregation methods to combine patch information from consecutive frames. The network's architecture is a modified version of MobileNetV2, with patch-based operations incorporated into existing blocks. The results show PatchNet outperforms other efficient models, including MobileNetV2, while requiring fewer computations and memory. Additionally, PatchNet achieves comparable performance to complex models on tasks such as video object detection and keyframe selection. We introduce an innovative method to decrease the resources required by such circuits, particularly those with looped structures, by leveraging their inherent ability to incorporate past information. Moiré patterns formed within twisted bilayers of two-dimensional semiconductors create unique conditions for interlayer excitons that can be influenced by a twist angle as low as 0.1 degrees. The resulting narrow bandwidths of optical emissions can be thousands of times smaller than their single-layer counterparts. However, understanding the underlying physics of these moiré systems remains a complex challenge. To address this, we have developed a method combining accurate mathematical frameworks for electronic and phonon interactions to study the optical properties of interlayer excitons. Our results show that in systems with small twist angles, the interlayer exciton bandwidth is controlled by a specific mathematical constant, the Euler's gamma constant. We also find that incorporating phonon interactions significantly affects the interlayer exciton binding energy, potentially making it weaker than previously thought. The presence of phonon interactions also leads to the interlayer exciton's decay rate being comparable to its binding energy. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the understanding of interlayer excitons in moiré systems. It also highlights the potential for future research to incorporate more complex factors, such as electronic and nuclear thermal motions, to further advance our understanding of these unique excitations. The advancement of Automated Reasoning within the Knowledge Engineering field has led to significant improvements in the quality of generated proof representations. These advancements have also sparked interest in the technological community, with proof generation now being utilized in various applications, including verification, program checking, and even educational tools. This study delves into the potential of proof generators as review assistants, exploring the challenges and opportunities that arise from incorporating them into the review process. To this end, we present a framework that facilitates the interaction between human reviewers and proof generators, enabling the detection of errors and omissions in generated material. This framework has been implemented and tested in a real review scenario within the Formal Methods community. Our findings indicate that, with minimal training, proof generators can effectively contribute to the review process, particularly by identifying oversights. This research sheds light on the potential benefits and obstacles of integrating proof generators into the review process, paving the way for future exploration in this domain. The enhanced method, employing early termination of inner iterations, allows for significant performance improvement by adapting to the convergence rate of successive over-relaxation algorithms. The termination criterion is based on the norm of residual vector, $\boldsymbol{r}$, and a corresponding convergence indicator, $\vartheta$. The interior point method without a preconditioner yields faster solution times than its preconditioned counterpart. One of the most computationally intensive tasks in bioinformatics is genomic sequence assembly. A key step in the assembly process is constructing a contig from overlapping DNA fragments, typically solved using integer programming. However, this approach only considers single fragments, neglecting potential multi-fragment combinations that could yield better results. In this paper, a multiway number partitioning extension of integer programming is introduced to enhance genomic sequence assembly. Computational experiments demonstrate that incorporating multi-fragment combinations accelerates and improves assembly quality, revealed through increased contig lengths and reduced gaps. The associated code is freely accessible on GitHub. In particular, the multiway number partitioning module is now included in the integer programming-based assembler, HiFlow-Assembler. As a result, the assembly time is reduced by a factor of 10 to 20, while the generated contigs are 10 to 50% longer than previous versions. Furthermore, the new approach outperforms state-of-the-art assemblers, such as Canu, FALCON, and WESP, in terms of contig length and accuracy. In particular, the longest contigs produced by HiFlow-Assembler are 20% to 50% longer than those of Canu, FALCON, and WESP. In addition, the new approach is 2 to 5 times more efficient than HiFlow-Assembler's single-fragment integer programming variant. In summary, the multiway number partitioning extension of integer programming significantly enhances genomic sequence assembly by increasing contig lengths, reducing gaps, and improving efficiency. We've conducted the first comprehensive examination of angular clustering statistics among LoTSS galaxies at 1.3 GHz. Our research focused on 50 massive halos from $0.05<z<0.6$, using 1,611 galaxies within a specific luminosity range. Our findings align with the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, demonstrating consistency with predicted galaxy distributions. We've also developed constraints on the mass scaling of angular clustering, yielding an $M-\delta_T^2$ relation index of $2.04\pm0.13$ and a $M_{\rm 500,3R_{500}}$ of $(1.01\pm0.04)\times M_{\rm 500}$, in good agreement with previous studies. Our results provide essential groundwork for future radio surveys at higher redshifts. Additionally, our analysis has allowed us to estimate the radio luminosity function at 1.3 GHz for $z=0.05-0.6$, complementing existing UV and optical studies. We've found that LoTSS radio luminosity functions exhibit a steeper low-mass slope than predicted by galaxy evolution models, while displaying a better fit to UV-optical data at higher luminosities. Our results also show that LoTSS radio luminosity functions are consistent with being redshift invariant. Furthermore, we've investigated the relationship between radio luminosity and stellar mass, discovering that LoTSS galaxies exhibit a higher specific radio luminosity than UV-optical selected galaxies at $z\sim0.6$. Our findings are also compared to predictions from galaxy evolution models, highlighting potential areas for improvement. Our research has provided significant insights into the properties of radio galaxies at $z\sim0.6$, paving the way for future studies with deeper, wider LoTSS coverage. We demonstrate that a unique global optimal method for controlling entropy production exists, which differs significantly from previous findings indicating multiple optimal methods for achieving high entropy production rates. Unlike entropy production rates, which can be maximized through sequential control, maximizing the entropy production increment (max-PI) requires simultaneous control. We also show that achieving max-PI is impossible in systems with only two or three control parameters, limiting its applicability. Nevertheless, it is possible to control entropy production incrementally when a system undergoes a transition from one stationary state to another, which we term the max-PI incremental control problem (MIPC). We successfully apply an advanced machine learning technique, an evolution strategy, to solve the MIPC in a variety of two-dimensional systems. Furthermore, we observe that the optimal protocols for max-PI and MIPC often bear a resemblance to each other, which we attribute to the protocols being guided by the quasi-static path. We also explore the relationship between the optimal protocols for entropy production and those for max-PI, discovering that they can diverge significantly in certain situations. To facilitate the efficient computation of optimal protocols, we develop a new approach based on the Legendre-Fenchel transform, which we successfully apply to achieve high entropy production rates. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the efficiency of the optimal protocols and their duration, which we find exhibits a universal scaling behavior. We also identify a lower limit for the efficiency of the optimal protocols, which we find to be a constant value in the systems we studied. A novel approach for estimating the error in coupled problems between a fluid and its surrounding solid or solid-fluid interface is presented. This method utilizes a dual-weighted residual technique and a posteriori error estimator developed within the context of the fluent solver in COMSOL Multiphysics. The solver is modified to enable error computation for coupled flow, solid and fluid-structure interaction, and structural optimization problems. Several numerical experiments are performed to verify the accuracy of the developed error estimator. Furthermore, a convergence study is carried out to confirm that the estimated error accurately reflects the true error. The proposed method is expected to facilitate reliable mesh refinement and optimization procedures within the COMSOL environment. A comprehensive implementation of the method is provided in an online supplementary document.

We investigate the formation of social groupings within a system where agents' opinions evolve over time in a one-dimensional space. Opinions are updated according to a simple rule: each time step, an agent randomly selects a neighbor's opinion, adopting it with a certain probability. We demonstrate that this system spontaneously generates enduring social clusters by analyzing the underlying dynamics. These clusters arise due to local interactions and opinion movements restricted by the system's boundaries, leading to prolonged periods of stagnation in opinion diversity within each group. We show that system properties such as group size, opinion variety, and system homogeneity follow predictable patterns as the system evolves. These findings are confirmed through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. Additionally, we explore strategies for assessing social groupings and their characteristics. One viable approach involves setting a threshold for opinion similarity, while another method utilizes a more complex clustering algorithm. We examine the implications of using these groupings for reducing echo chambers and increasing opinion diversity within the groups. Our results indicate that both methods are effective in achieving these goals, though the more complex approach tends to perform better. Crucially, we identify a system parameter that determines whether these group assessment methods are capable of improving opinion diversity. We also explore the potential for agents to influence one another's opinions by sharing information, represented by adding a 'information' parameter that represents the frequency of such events. Our analysis reveals that this parameter can significantly impact the system's dynamics, leading to the emergence of more uniform groupings with greater diversity in opinions. Furthermore, we examine the distribution of opinions within the system, finding that its structure can be accurately described by a specific probability distribution under certain conditions. Our work contributes to the understanding of how opinion dynamics give rise to social clusters, and we provide a framework for evaluating these groupings and improving them. Our findings also shed light on the interplay between system parameters and the resulting social structures, offering avenues for manipulating this social architecture. Ultimately, our research may inspire new methods for identifying and utilizing social groupings in real-world applications. To that end, our code is available for reproduction of our results. The time between the completion of transcription and the generation of mature mRNA is influenced by multiple factors, including promoter activity, RNA processing, and messenger RNA export. To investigate this period, researchers employed live-cell imaging of a green fluorescent protein in yeast, specifically focusing on a gene of varying lengths. The findings revealed that the length of a gene significantly affects the time between transcription completion and the appearance of mature mRNA, with longer genes exhibiting more pronounced effects. A mathematical model was developed to simulate RNA export and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms. It was discovered that short genes are exported by one ribonucleotide complex at a time, whereas longer genes are exported by multiple complexes working together. The model also showed that RNA processing is not a major contributor to the observed gene-length dependent delay. Instead, the primary cause is the time required for the export of the initial short region of longer genes. Notably, the model's results are consistent across different gene lengths and can be quantified using a single parameter, the rate at which one ribonucleotide complex can travel during RNA export. Using a robotic hand to pick up everyday objects, humans successfully integrate multiple sensory inputs like vision, touch, and sound. Current research on object identification after dropping has primarily focused on a single sensory channel, vision. In this work, we explore the fusion of multi-modal sensory information to identify dropped objects. We developed a novel, multi-modal fusion approach for object identification, combining vision, sound, and inertial measurements from a falling object. Our approach consists of two main components: a feature extraction system and a fusion module. The feature extraction system uses deep learning to extract features from each sensory input, and the fusion module fuses these extracted features using a simple yet effective method. Our results show that the integration of multi-modal sensory information significantly improves object identification accuracy compared to using a single sensory channel. For instance, combining all three sensory inputs increased the identification accuracy by 15% compared to using vision alone. Our approach was tested using a custom-built droppable object system, which mimics real-world scenarios and provides diverse sensory inputs. Our research demonstrates that object identification can be successfully performed using multi-modal sensory information, and we provide a framework for future research on this topic. For search-related tasks, public sector professionals may rely on Google's search engine as their primary source of information. However, Web search algorithm biases can significantly impact search outcomes, which public sector professionals need to avoid. To address this, our research involves analyzing algorithmic biases in Google's search results that public sector professionals are likely to encounter. We conducted experiments to demonstrate biases in search outcomes and developed a framework to help public sector professionals recognize potential biases in Google's search results. This framework consists of a set of questions that these professionals can use to identify potential biases in search outcomes. We also gathered data on how public sector professionals in Germany perceive algorithmic biases in Web search. Our results indicate that many of these professionals are unaware of potential biases in Google's search results and could benefit from our framework and the associated questions in their work. Furthermore, our research involves discussing potential challenges and limitations of using our framework in practice. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the responsibilities of Web search algorithm developers in addressing algorithmic biases. The program synthesis framework, introduced by Ghelfan and Ghezzi in 1981, synthesizes a program by generating possible programs, executing them against specifications, and selecting the first one that meets all requirements. We've re-examined the performance of this framework using a modern computing system and a set of real-world benchmarks. Our results show that, on average, program synthesis takes only a few milliseconds, but can occasionally take several minutes. A statistical analysis of synthesis times reveals that they follow a lognormal distribution. Furthermore, we've developed a model that accurately predicts synthesis times based on program size and the number of specifications. This model has a 95% confidence level and can be used to estimate synthesis times for new scenarios. Overall, our findings suggest that program synthesis is a feasible approach, but its performance can vary significantly depending on the specific context. To facilitate future research, we're releasing our findings and the program synthesis framework as open-source software. The JCMT is poised to observe key molecular emission lines at 13CO, 12CO, and CO, which will significantly aid in the study of GWPCs. Estimating scene geometry can be a more effective approach to pre-training than image classification, yet current self-supervised learning methods for geometry estimation are limited by their focus on a single viewpoint. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach that utilizes a two-view geometry task to generate rich, 3D scene representations. Our method, which we call Two-View Net, leverages a two-stream encoder to process both input images and generates a more comprehensive 3D representation compared to single-view methods. By doing so, it becomes easier to extract useful features from any image viewpoint. Moreover, our method can be easily extended to other geometry estimation tasks such as depth estimation and pose-based semantic segmentation by adjusting the projection module. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art single-view methods in both self-supervised and supervised settings. Additionally, it exhibits better performance than pose-conditioned methods in depth estimation. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhenglei1994/TwoView-Net.

We introduce a novel computational method for creating dark matter halos with cores, allowing for a vast range of possible masses. This method is an extension of previous work by Bringkat et al. and forms part of a larger project to generate diverse dark matter halo profiles. The core-based halo generator produces isotropic halos using a two-step process: first, it generates a mass-based boundary, and then determines the core's radius through an iterative algorithm. The core's mass is calculated based on the remaining mass within the boundary. The core-based generator enables the creation of halos with cores on a massive scale, and our preliminary findings indicate that such halos can account for a significant portion of galaxy rotation curve diversity. The generator will be utilized to investigate the implications of core-based halos on galaxy evolution, and their potential to explain a substantial amount of rotation curve diversity. The core-based halo generator will be made publicly available on GitHub under the name CBHG.

To effectively encourage personal climate action, it is crucial to comprehend how people's core values relate to their willingness to take action. This study presents a value-based model that predicts an individual's climate action motivation by first identifying their personal values and then assessing how these values align with action-related values. The model was developed using a large dataset of responses from the California Climate Survey and validated with data from a subsequent survey. The results indicate that the model accurately forecasts an individual's motivation to take climate action, as supported by a significant and interpretable finding from a Random Forest analysis. Furthermore, the model's values-based approach provides actionable insights for encouraging climate action among specific segments of the population. For instance, people who prioritize social relationships and security are more likely to be motivated to take climate action if they are reminded of the economic benefits of individual actions. The model's framework can be adapted to study other issues by replacing the climate action construct with a different one. Additionally, the study's findings highlight the significance of personal core values in influencing behavior and the importance of considering individual values when developing effective policies. We analyze survivor sets resulting from various intermediate beta-transformations and demonstrate that each corresponds to a subset of badly approximable numbers in a specific non-integer base. This conclusion stems from a general theorem, applicable to a broad class of transformations defined by Rauzy fractions, whose proof relies on prior work by Christensen and Peres on local mixing properties. As a specific instance of our theoretical outcome, we re-examine the survivor sets associated with beta-transformations at golden ratios and Fibonacci numbers, obtaining results analogous to those previously established by Trakhanson. Furthermore, our method allows us to compute the Hausdorff dimension of the survivor sets resulting from arbitrary beta-transformations, extending the work of Darlow, Mauldin, and Trakhanson in a particular case. Additionally, we provide a distinct proof of a dimension result for the survivor sets associated with beta-transformations at golden ratios and Fibonacci numbers. Lastly, we investigate the Hausdorff dimension of the survivor sets resulting from Moran constructions in arbitrary non-integer bases, a field of study previously explored by Mauldin and Strichartz in the context of rational bases. In scanning transmission electron microscopy, electrostatic phase plates are used to modify the electron beam, but the choice of design specifications significantly affects their performance. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of different phase plate designs to determine their optimal configuration. Various fill-factors and pixel patterns are examined to minimize the size of the electron probe while maximizing its current density. The results indicate that a fill-factor of 0.5 and a pixel pattern of two adjacent holes per unit cell yield the best outcomes. Additionally, the study provides a straightforward method for designing phase plates with specified properties. The findings of this research will guide the development of improved phase plates for various electron microscopy applications. Furthermore, the study's design principles can be applied to other electron optical systems. The associated design software is available for download at https://github.com/keith-harrison/design-ESP.

Recent advancements in end-to-end text-to-speech systems have led to significant improvements in synthesized speech quality. However, current systems still struggle to capture speech's inherent disorder, such as filler words and speech interruptions, which are crucial for natural expression. To address this, we've developed MaskedSpeech, a novel system that leverages masked autoencoding to preserve speech patterns during training. By incorporating explicit masking, MaskedSpeech effectively retains speech characteristics, outperforming previous methods in naturalness and expressiveness while maintaining comparable fidelity. Our system also enables the synthesis of novel, unseen speech patterns, demonstrating its potential for open-world speech learning applications. Notably, MaskedSpeech achieves state-of-the-art results on the MOSiSA dataset, a benchmark focused on speech naturalness and expressiveness. This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach to variable selection that builds on sparse Bayesian linear regression by iteratively adding and removing variables from a model. We begin with a prior distribution for model coefficients that utilizes a complex prior for variance and a product of two simple priors for means and variances, enabling posterior inference using the Relevance Vector Machine algorithm. Each iteration of the process involves drawing a new variable from the selected model and updating the posterior distribution, ensuring that uncertainties are retained by conditioning the distribution on the previously chosen variables. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in choosing relevant variables and achieving sparse solutions on artificial and real-world datasets. Notably, this approach outperforms competing methods in a simulation study, and its computational expense is comparable to that of lasso and elastic net methods. Additionally, we provide a theoretical justification for the method in a supplementary document. Deep Neural Network (DNN) vulnerabilities to adversarial examples have gained significant research attention. Most studies focus on targeted attacks that aim to mislead a model into classifying an input as a specific, incorrect class. Unlike conventional approaches, Man-in-the-Middle attacks redirect incoming traffic to a different destination without involving the actual target. We're the first to apply adversarial techniques to network security, specifically transforming URLs to redirect users to malicious sites. Our research investigates the effectiveness of various attacks on different defenses across multiple URL transformation methods. Interestingly, the most successful attacks often involve minimal changes to the original URL. Additionally, we propose a simple yet efficient method to prevent URL adversarial attacks and demonstrate its efficacy through experiments. Our findings and resource are available at url-defender.github.io.

Climate change is a pressing global issue, but social media platforms are filled with conspiracy theories that confuse the public about its existence and severity. Our research focuses on the climate change denial group, analyzing their activity on Twitter and identifying their most popular engagement strategies from January 2020 to June 2021. Our results show that this group consists mainly of far-right ideologies and consist of repeat offenders, revealing a pattern of coordinated behavior when analyzing their retweet networks. We also found that their most effective engagement methods involve using emotive language and sharing high-quality visuals. Interestingly, we discovered that conspiracy theory-related content about climate change is largely driven by a single group, suggesting the potential for platforms to target and restrict their activity. Our research highlights the need for platforms to address the root causes of the problem, including the involvement of multiple accounts held by the same individuals, in order to effectively combat the harmful effects of climate change-related misinformation on Twitter. Our findings can inform the development of more effective strategies to address the issue. We also introduce ClimateCheck, a tool that can be used to monitor the activity of the climate change denial group and provide insights into their behavior. This study compares the economic return on investment for different higher education fields in Norway and Denmark. Both countries have publicly available data on earnings by field, but also on student demographics, allowing us to control for individual characteristics. Our analysis reveals that Norwegian fields of study yield significantly higher earnings payoffs than those in Denmark. Upon closer examination, we find that these results can be partly attributed to existing student characteristics. Additionally, we identify that Norwegian fields with lower earnings payoffs are dominated by female students, whereas fields with higher earnings payoffs are predominantly chosen by males. Our findings have implications for how fields of study are marketed and encouraged in both countries. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering individual preferences when making educational choices. Due to data limitations, we are unable to explore other potential factors that may influence these choices, such as personal interests or the potential for self-employment. Nonetheless, our analysis provides a more nuanced understanding of how to compare the return on investment for different higher education fields in Norway and Denmark. Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that students choose fields of study based on a trade-off between earnings and personal preferences. To validate this hypothesis, we utilize data on the specific fields of study that students choose in both countries. Our analysis reveals that students in both Norway and Denmark prioritize fields with high non-monetary rewards and those that offer good earnings prospects, but instead of maximizing overall return on investment, students appear to be seeking a balance between these two factors. Our research also demonstrates that students in both countries are more willing to forgo higher earnings in fields with high non-monetary rewards, but that this willingness to forgo earnings is greater among Norwegian students. Our analysis further shows that students in both countries are more inclined to sacrifice higher earnings in fields preferred by a higher proportion of their peers. To account for the potential influence of peer effects, we employ an instrumental variable approach. Our results indicate that Norwegian students are more responsive to changes in the peer preference of fields of study compared to Danish students. Our research also reveals that students in both countries are more inclined to sacrifice higher earnings in fields that are preferred by a higher proportion of their local peers. To account for the potential influence of local environmental factors, we utilize data on the geographic distribution of students in both countries. Our analysis shows that Norwegian students are more responsive to local peer effects compared to Danish students. Our research highlights the importance of considering local conditions when making educational choices. To further validate our findings, we also explore the potential influence of family background on field of study choices in both countries.

We examine the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, introducing an adaptation to the model for improved segmentation of corrupted images. Unbiased image recovery is combined with the segmentation task by dividing the model into two parts: one addresses the segmentation and image recovery, while the other enforces the segmentation constraint through a penalized term. Our approach splits the process into iterative, computationally efficient steps: a convex image recovery phase and a non-convex segmentation phase. Convergence to a stable point is achieved through the use of a proximal point algorithm. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our method in segmenting images affected by noise, outliers, and various forms of corruption. Additionally, comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods highlight our approach as a robust solution. Due to its complexity, the theoretical convergence of our method requires further research. We've explored the possibility of ultra-light scalar, vector, and pseudoscalar fields influencing the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data. To do this, we utilized a model where these fields interact with baryons through a Yukawa potential, and our analysis revealed the impact of a Yukawa potential on Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, setting limits on the phase space density of these fields. Our findings suggest that if ultra-light particles make up all of dark matter, their abundance is below the Peccei-Quinn symmetry-breaking scale raised to the power of 1.08, and is instead constrained by a relationship with the baryon density. This constraint is more stringent than previous estimates. We've also discovered that if ultra-light particles constitute a portion of dark matter, the maximum possible fraction is inversely proportional to the mass of the particle. The results show that this new learning method is comparable to traditional spike-prop in both accuracy and computational requirements. This research proposes an innovative method to restore severely degraded document images using a combination of handwritten Text Recognition and Generative Adversarial Networks. The approach involves using a pre-trained Text Recognizer to generate text features from the original document images, which are then fed into a Generative Adversarial Network to produce enhanced images based on these features. The restored images are represented as differences between the original images and the generated features, rather than being directly generated from scratch. The quality of the restored images can be evaluated using the generated text, resulting in significant improvements over previous methods. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through successful restoration of real document images. The source code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alexeymishin/TextImageEnhancement.

Current deep learning approaches for SR typically rely on high-quality datasets and are not well-suited for astronomical images. By comparing its performance to existing SR techniques, we show that it yields more detailed and accurate galaxy images, with improved results when using only a small number of input frames. This approach has potential applications in real-world astronomical research, and could be used to improve images captured by future space telescopes. We also provide a Python implementation of this method, making it accessible to researchers. This paper introduces a novel neural network algorithm that enhances the performance of backpropagation by limiting the rate at which model parameters change during training. By capping modifications to weights and introducing a localized, adaptive 'noise' component, the network reduces overfitting and its associated tendency to follow noisy patterns in the data. Theoretical analysis confirms the efficacy of this approach, and experimental results demonstrate improved performance relative to standard techniques across multiple benchmark datasets. Notably, this algorithm achieves superior results on complex image classification tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods that utilize transfer learning. Knowledge graph link prediction is a key aspect of graph completion that uses information from existing triples to forecast non-existent ones. Current approaches often build upon relation extraction data by utilizing it to initialize parameters and incorporating it into complex architectures. However, these methods neglect to explicitly leverage relation extraction data when making link prediction, despite it being a crucial aspect of knowledge graphs. To address this, we introduce a method that utilizes relation extraction data to initialize parameters and also directly incorporates it into link prediction, leveraging the extracted information of entire relations. The success of deep learning stems from its versatility as a learning paradigm, yet its geometric underpinnings remain poorly understood. Revealing the intrinsic geometry of deep learning models can provide valuable insights, enabling the development of more effective algorithms and architectures. In this paper, we present a novel approach to visualizing the geometry of deep learning models, specifically residual networks, using persistent homology. By applying this method to residual networks, we show that it is possible to represent them as metric spaces, thereby allowing for topological analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that residual layers exhibit a universal geometric characteristic, independent of the specific network, and that distortions in this geometry are associated with performance degradation. Our findings provide a foundation for using topological analysis in evaluating the effectiveness of deep learning models. Additionally, we show that persistent homology can be utilized for training and adaptation purposes. Specifically, we utilize the distortion of the residual layer's geometry as a regularization term in the loss function, enabling the learning of compact and effective residual networks. Moreover, we show that residual layers with specific geometric characteristics can be selectively removed during training, leading to improved performance. Our approach is further validated by its application in adapting pre-trained models to various datasets, resulting in the removal of irrelevant features and the enhancement of the models' overall performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/krishnanvatsalya/deep_homology. Our results are presented in the supplementary material. This research investigates the adaptability of pre-trained language models to novel languages, exploring the effect of varying amounts of data and different training settings on this adaptability. A thorough analysis is conducted to understand the adaptability process and its outcomes, using a range of evaluation metrics. The findings are further utilized to create a predictive framework for anticipating adaptability levels. The data and code for this study are openly available. 

Here are the key results:
- A pre-defined dataset is established for adapting English LMs to Romanian, comprising 10,000 sentences.
- Using this dataset, a pre-trained Romanian language model is successfully adapted, achieving performance superior to a Romanian model trained from scratch on the Romanian dataset.
- The relationship between data size and adaptability is examined, revealing a non-linear correlation.
- Different training settings, such as fine-tuning vs. prompt-based adaptation, are tested and their effects on adaptability are explored.
- A novel framework is developed to forecast the adaptability of a target language based on the similarity between its and a source language.
- The framework is validated across multiple language pairs, demonstrating a strong correlation between predicted and actual adaptability levels.

This paper introduces a novel, m-arithmetic version of the kappa (m-ar-K) function, a dimensionality reduction technique derived from the kernel trick. Building upon previous work, the m-ar-K function offers enhanced performance over its arithmetic mean-based counterpart, with applications in multi-label classification, particularly for datasets with large label sets and sparse labels. We present an iterative algorithm for calculating multi-label kernel matrices and demonstrate the m-ar-K function's superiority over existing methods on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the m-ar-K function is combined with the singular value decomposition (SVD) to enhance multi-label classification models. The proposed method is denoted as m-ar-KLPS and is compared to state-of-the-art techniques in an empirical study. The results show that m-ar-KLPS outperforms existing methods across various label complexity measures and dataset types. The quality of informed debate on social media significantly influences public opinion. Yet, most current approaches for social media analysis focus on individual posts, neglecting the underlying narratives that drive discussion. In this paper, the challenges and opportunities of narrative-based social media analysis are explored, along with a proposed framework for identifying narratives and assessing their impact. Evaluations within the academic and broader news contexts demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. By applying this framework, the structure of narratives and their evolution over time can be mapped, enabling policymakers and the general public to make more informed decisions by engaging with the prevailing narratives. Furthermore, this analysis can facilitate the identification of supporting and opposing narratives, enabling the quantification of narrative influence and the detection of shifts in public opinion. In particular, our study reveals that the narratives surrounding COVID-19 vaccine adoption were dominated by only a few themes and involved a distinct set of users. In contrast, the analysis of news articles on this topic shows a more extensive set of narratives with less influence from individual users. These findings underscore the value of our approach in uncovering the underlying narratives in social media posts and news content. In the future, this framework can be adapted to various domains by incorporating domain-specific knowledge to enhance its performance. Additionally, the use of NLP techniques can be further optimized by integrating more advanced models, such as transformer-based architectures. Ultimately, the narratives identified through our approach can inform more targeted interventions to shape public opinion. In the context of news, the analysis of narratives can aid journalists in discovering underreported themes and constructing more compelling stories. We introduce a new framework that guarantees the robustness of deep learning models in the face of adverse perturbations. This framework, which incorporates a layer-wise defense mechanism, relies on a nested set of constraints that limit potential input variations. By formulating an optimization problem with these constraints, we can train models that are robust to extreme perturbations while maintaining accuracy on normal inputs. Our approach is inspired by the concept of worst-case averaging and builds on existing research in adversarial training. We evaluate its effectiveness on standard image classification datasets, achieving notable results. The associated code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alexalexalex1/RobustDeepLearning.

including PCA, MDA, CCA, t-SNE, AE, LE, UMAP, and DCA, in a signal 
reconstruction context. It specifically compares their performance in a 
hyperspectral pixel classification task using the UAv-S2 dataset. The results

contribution of this research involves transforming these methods into 
semi-supervised algorithms by integrating them with k-NN and EM labels propagation 
techniques. The combined methods are then tested on various hyperspectral 
datasets, yielding improved classification results compared to their unsupervised 
counterparts and other semi-supervised algorithms. The research also includes 
comparisons with deep learning approaches. The code and data used in this study

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various applications but face significant challenges due to their substantial size, which necessitates considerable storage space and computation power. Consequently, developing efficient model compression techniques has become a pressing research area. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in compressing deep neural networks, focusing on pruning, quantization, and other related methods. Moreover, we introduce a novel framework for compressive learning, which encompasses both compressing models and adapting datasets. In addition, we discuss the key challenges and propose potential future directions for further improvement. Our goal is to stimulate research in this domain and encourage the development of a unified framework for compressive learning. Our work is expected to contribute to both theoretical and practical aspects of compressing deep neural networks. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Eyck/compressive-learning.

In the context of Generative Adversarial Networks, the choice of loss function significantly influences the model's performance. While cross-entropy is frequently utilized due to its ease of implementation and connection to information theory, other loss functions like KL divergence remain underrepresented. This study delves into the effects of using KL divergence for both discriminative and generative tasks in the context of semi-supervised classification and image generation. Our findings reveal that, contrary to cross-entropy, KL divergence can result in inferior outcomes. To address this, we introduce a modified approach to the loss function and demonstrate its ability to enhance model performance. Our work is expected to contribute to a more thorough comprehension of the capabilities and limitations of various loss functions in the context of GANs. We examine the Hamiltonian-derived model of parquet theory, comparing its amplitude to the conventional parquet amplitude obtained via integral equations. Notably, the former preserves Hamiltonian and crossing symmetry, whereas the latter only satisfies crossing symmetry. We demonstrate that the standard parquet approach fails to conserve the Hamiltonian due to an incorrect assumption in its derivation. To resolve this issue, we introduce an alternative derivation for the parquet approach, yielding a more robust form that exhibits the correct Hamiltonian conservation. However, this new version fails to meet the conventional requirements for its bare and self-energy components. We address these discrepancies and provide a more robust definition of parquet theory, ensuring its conservation and crossing symmetry properties. We also apply this new framework to compute the S-matrix for the SU(N) Wilson Fermion model. Interestingly, the derived S-matrix shows a significant difference when compared to the standard parquet result, particularly in its conservation properties. We provide a detailed analysis of the origins of these differences. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of conserving Hamiltonian symmetry in the construction of parquet theory. We also discuss the implications of our work for the application of parquet theory to lattice field theories. Given its robustness, we suggest the derived model as a suitable candidate for the parquet approximation of QED. We further explore its potential for use in non-relativistic theories, such as QED3 and QED1+1. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extending our new framework to SU(N) Wilson Fermion model with N=3, a case that has practical significance for lattice field theories. Finally, we discuss the prospect of generalizing our approach to Fermi surfaces with arbitrary SU(N) symmetries. Active learning algorithms are designed to efficiently select a limited number of data points for labeling by a human annotator, maximizing learning gain. Traditional methods rely on an iterative query process, but their computational expense makes them impractical for large datasets. We present a novel, scalable approach to active learning that overcomes the drawbacks of previous methods. This semi-supervised, entropy-based method is a flexible extension of existing minimax entropy-based active learning algorithms. It addresses the issue of selecting data points that are both uncertain and diverse by first identifying the most uncertain samples and then refining the selection by considering diversity. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric to gauge sample diversity. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets, achieving comparable performance on large datasets at a significantly lower computational cost. This study analyzes the distinctiveness of sound textures in popular music from the 1960s to the present day. A dataset of 1000 songs, spanning five decades, was created by extracting audio segments. Characterizing each song's sound texture using a dimensionality-reduced representation, the study discovered that songs within the same period exhibit similarities in their sound texture profiles. Interestingly, the sound of music from the 1960s is distinct from music of the 2000s, but songs from adjacent decades show gradual changes in their sound texture. The findings suggest that the sound of music evolves in waves, with new decades initially adopting characteristics from previous periods before developing distinct features. The study's data and code are accessible via open-source platforms.

This article explores the concept of semantic implication within proof-theoretic semantics. Initially, we consider various notions of semantic implication derived from different proof-theoretic operations such as cut elimination, conservativity, and translation. The article then introduces a containment relationship among these operations and shows that, for a given class of logical systems, there is a maximum notion of semantic implication reflecting both containment and converse relationships. This concept is analogous to the fundamental theorem in proof-theoretic semantics but is presented in a more general form applicable to diverse classes of logical systems. Furthermore, we examine specific instances of such general theorems for natural deduction and sequent calculus. The article also discusses the relationship between semantic implication and other proof-theoretic notions such as computationally meaningful operations and reflection principles. We investigate how utilizing human feedback efficiently in the reward learning process can significantly minimize training time. Presently, most systems process human feedback one comparison at a time. We introduce an innovative method where these comparisons are processed in batches, enabling substantial improvements in learning velocity. By grouping comparisons within a batch based on their expected impact on the model, we create a queue that is drained in a way that maximizes the learning gain. This batching technique is combined with an analysis of the comparisons within each batch to provide even greater efficiency gains. Our system, known as BSL, is shown to outperform current state-of-the-art systems in both theoretical and practical evaluations. Furthermore, an in-depth examination of BSL reveals its potential to function as an optimal within-batch comparison processor. This technique has the potential to be scaled up to process human feedback in more complex reward learning tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexeyguz/BSL. Additionally, a video illustrating the system can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q8Q6Q8Q8Q.

A Bayesian approach to modeling extreme values is proposed, using a Poisson process with spatially correlated defects, to analyze potential failure times. The prior distribution for the correlation matrix is set as an inverse Wishart distribution with scale matrix parameters, allowing for the exploration of different levels of spatial dependence. The method relies on a block Gibbs sampler for simulation, using a tuning parameter m to determine the size of each block, which can impact convergence speed. The impact of m is investigated and guidelines for its selection are provided. The method is applied to real-world data on hydraulic fracture propagation, demonstrating its ability to identify key factors influencing potential failure risk. Further analysis involves estimating the potential failure times and their associated probabilities, as well as developing a diagnostic tool to identify areas of highest failure risk. The method is made available through an R package, extremeBayes.

We have developed a set of robust algorithms for reinforcement learning in situations where an adversary may be manipulating the reward functions. Our approach ensures that these algorithms remain effective by providing guarantees on performance regardless of the extent of corruption, which must be known in advance. We have created algorithms for both finite and infinite Markov decision processes that offer high reward values, which remain within a certain percentage margin, with the percentage determined by the level of corruption. These results improve upon existing methods, which required knowledge of corruption levels but provided only general effectiveness assurances. We have also established a lower bound on performance, which shows that our algorithms are optimal given certain conditions regarding the structure of MDPs. We have tested our methods on various tasks, which demonstrate their ability to withstand significant levels of corruption. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/alexeyguzk/robust_rl. Identifying out-of-distribution data is a critical task that has garnered interest recently. Current detection methods, which rely on pre-computed density models, struggle when faced with challenge data in robustness tests. This study proposes a new method that excels in detecting unseen data and requires minimal adjustments to existing code. It utilizes a pre-trained model to generate pseudo-labelling for unlabeled test data, then trains a classifier to identify anomalies based on these pseudo-labels. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on specific datasets but also demonstrates robustness on new challenge data. Furthermore, it offers valuable pseudo-labels that can aid in identifying data discrepancies. Our method and additional resources are available at https://github.com/alexeygoolchian/ood_pseudo_labeling.

We investigate whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be converted into a one-way transducer, using a specific, regular, and bounded synchronizer, preserving origin. This synchronizer is defined by a regular language that specifies when two states in the original and target transducers are equivalent. This problem is known to be decidable, but we present an alternative, more complex decision procedure than the one previously established. Additionally, we demonstrate that if the synchronizer language is not bounded, it cannot be defined by a regular expression, and we present an example that supports this finding. Furthermore, we explore the synchronizability of language classes, including one-way, two-way, and multi-way transducers, and provide new insights and results for these classes. Finally, we examine the complexity of synchronizing a non-deterministic two-way automaton and present a decision procedure with a higher complexity. This study contributes new knowledge to the field. We have conducted a study of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, a gas giant located in a binary system, to understand how it forms. This is significant because GJ 229B is an intermediate object that shares characteristics with both planets and stars. To analyze its atmosphere, we used the NaCO2 and NaH absorption bands in the near-infrared spectrum obtained with the IRTF, Mauna Kea, Hawaii. This spectrum was taken at a time when GJ 229B was in a state of high activity. Our analysis indicates that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is composed of 0.5-1.5% sodium, 0.1-0.5% potassium, and 0.1-0.5% calcium. We also found that the cloud properties of GJ 229B are similar to those of UMa c, with a particle size of 0.1-1 micrometers and a scale height of 0.5-1.5 times the hydrostatic scale height. Our model shows that the cloud is composed of 10^-4 g/cm^3 particles, which is consistent with the theory of grain formation in protoplanetary disks. Our findings suggest that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is primarily influenced by the evaporation of super-saturated clouds and the sedimentation of small particles. This is consistent with the theory of gas giant formation through core accretion. This is supported by the detection of a H-alpha emission line, which indicates that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is still interacting with the disk. This is the first time that the atmosphere of GJ 229B has been studied in detail, which provides new insights into its formation process. We introduce a parameterized algorithm framework for directed acyclic graphs based on their treewidth, building on the semidefinite programming approach developed by Alon et al. In this approach, we utilize eigenvalue-free semidefinite programming to solve a parameterized version of a certain directed acyclic graph problem in o(2^tw n) time, where tw represents the treewidth and n denotes the number of vertices. This methodology yields novel parameterized results for several acyclic graph problems, including the longest path, minimum profit path, and minimum weight perfect fractional matching problems. Furthermore, we derive a parameterized semidefinite programming algorithm for general graphs based on the treewidth of their primal and dual elimination graphs. This discovery leads to novel parameterized results for the minimum weight perfect fractional matching problem. This work significantly expands the scope of semidefinite programming in parameterized algorithmics. In particular, it offers the first semidefinite programming parameterized algorithm for the minimum weight perfect fractional matching problem. This improvement is particularly notable since semidefinite programming has historically been considered inefficient in general graphs. Self-supervised approaches to point cloud-based global localization and navigation in dynamic environments are often limited to two-dimensional navigation. However, 3D navigation is essential for tasks such as autonomous driving and drone navigation. Current 3D methods rely on complex and expensive 3D reconstruction techniques, hindering efficient and real-time navigation in complex scenarios. To address this, we introduce MemoNav, a self-supervised 3D navigation method that leverages a memory-based attention mechanism to directly utilize 3D point clouds for global localization and mapping in dynamic environments. By focusing on relevant features within a pre-processed map, MemoNav outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods in 3D navigation while maintaining real-time capabilities. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuepeng/MemoNav. To our knowledge, this is the first paper on self-supervised 3D point cloud-based navigation. which sub-tree is used for a given input, emulating an adversarial 
process. Conversely, models like GANs use an adversarial training method

identification of unreliable models and (2) the creation of proxy models, 
which can be used for model distillation. Our method is demonstrated
