This study examines how giving students partial feedback influences their behavior when working on a programming assignment. We experiment with providing students with feedback on either the quality of their code or the correctness of its output, and observe their behavior twice: once immediately after receiving feedback, and again after viewing a graph showing code coverage for their submission. The positions of lines highlighted in this graph indicate areas of the code the student used while running it. We compare the results of these two trials to understand how the form of feedback given affects student behavior and, in turn, the effectiveness of the feedback. Our analysis shows that providing feedback on code quality encourages students to explore more of the available code, leading to better performance in terms of code coverage and higher programming grades. Conversely, output-focused feedback tends to limit the areas of the code the students use. Notably, when given the opportunity to adjust their approach based on code coverage feedback, students who initially received output-focused feedback are able to utilize more of the available code, bridging the gap in performance seen earlier. This finding suggests that providing students with feedback on code quality can have long-lasting effects that improve their programming skills. We also identify a group of students who are resistant to changing their approach based on feedback, and observe that these students tend to perform poorly in terms of code coverage and quality. Our results have implications for how to design and implement feedback mechanisms that can motivate students to improve their coding techniques. We also propose several potential variations of the code coverage feedback that could be explored in future studies. Ultimately, our study contributes to our understanding of how to effectively use code coverage as a tool to educate students and improve their programming abilities. By providing insights into the behavior of students working on a programming assignment, our study also sheds light on the underlying cognitive processes involved in the problem-solving activities of novice programmers. Over-smoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) is a significant challenge that restricts the applicability of deep learning methods in graph classification. While existing solutions aim to address over-smoothing, they lack a clear theoretical foundation. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of over-smoothing, offering a new perspective that considers residual connections, non-linear activations, and graph structures. Based on this understanding, we introduce a novel approach to prevent over-smoothing and present supporting experimental results. Furthermore, we show that the widely adopted GCN architecture is prone to over-smoothing due to its inherent properties. By dissecting the graph classification task into high-level and low-level features, we are able to identify and quantify the contributions of different GCN components. Ultimately, our research sheds light on the underlying causes of over-smoothing and offers a theoretical framework for the development of more robust algorithms. We introduce a novel deep learning strategy that utilizes cardiac activity signals to guide the extraction of meaningful echocardiogram image features, thereby enhancing the detection of cardiac abnormalities even in noisy environments. The proposed method involves two interconnected components: a cardiac activation representation learning module and a feature extraction module. The former leverages cardiac activity signals to derive a cardiac activation map, while the latter utilizes this map to enhance echocardiogram image features. A fusion network then combines the enriched image features with the original cardiac activity signals to generate a combined representation, which is used for downstream tasks. Notably, the method can be trained end-to-end without the need for paired data. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the method's superiority over state-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation approaches. This study explores the connection between flavor irregularities in meson systems and lepton-flavor universality violations in the Wilsonian effective low-energy theory. We consider a minimal scenario where new physics only affects the up, down, and charm quarks at a scale below 1 GeV. Our findings suggest that, in this context, the source of these violations is linked to a type of universality breaking in the lepton sector, specifically in the neutrino mass matrix. We also examine the potential impact of this scenario on lepton-sectored new physics searches. Moreover, we outline a systematic approach to analyzing flavor data within the Wilsonian EFT framework and apply it to the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ and $B^0$-$\overline{B^0}$ systems. Our results demonstrate that, in this effective theory, the flavor data can be represented by a set of physically interpretable parameters. We use this formalism to re-analyze the data and identify its constraints on the Wilson coefficients. Our analysis reveals that the constraints on certain Wilson coefficients are comparable to those derived from the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. We also identify potential signs of new physics in the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ and $B^0$-$\overline{B^0}$ mixing data. Our study highlights the utility of the Wilsonian EFT in analyzing flavor data and its potential to shed light on the nature of new physics. We introduce QASPER, a large-scale dataset of 1.5 million questions that complements existing datasets by providing answers for questions that would otherwise be labeled as out-of-domain. Current NLP models struggle with unknown words, but our dataset enables research into how models can infer the meanings of unfamiliar terms in a question. Our analysis reveals that existing models are not only poor at unknown words but also prone to misinterpreting them, often by shifting towards a nearby word in the vocabulary. To address this, we propose a new approach that uses the word's context to determine its likely semantic neighborhood, effectively limiting model guesswork. Our results show this method outperforms a simple baseline in a new evaluation metric. Our dataset and accompanying code are publicly available.

Recent advancements in deep learning technology have significantly improved the classification of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). However, most studies rely on comprehensive datasets, which are not always readily available in real-world clinical settings due to privacy concerns. This study presents a novel approach to train ADHD classifiers using a significantly reduced subset of relevant regions of interest. Additionally, the study introduces a new metric to evaluate the importance of regions of interest. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of the DSGRU model in classifying ADHD from a highly reduced dataset, making it a more practical solution for real-world clinical applications. We investigate the topological nature of nodal lines in solids, occurring in momentum space. Unlike other topological states, nodal lines aren't characterized by a number, but rather its direction in momentum space. This leads to a novel classification using a "homology group" of a nodal line's path. Through this approach, we can determine the topological properties of solids with nodal lines and study how they change when the material transforms into another form, called a phase transition. Our study shows that nodal lines can exist in both flat materials, made up of atoms repeated in two dimensions, and materials with extra dimensions. It also shows that nodal lines can be found on a single surface of a material, even if it's not a flat surface. This is demonstrated in a new material, consisting of atoms of YSb$_3$ in a honeycomb structure. Our findings show that this material has a topological property, called a Z$_2$ number, of 1, indicating it can be used to detect quasiparticles called Weyl points. Identifying planetary events in Kepler data is crucial for understanding the distribution of planetary mass ratios, which has significant implications for the field of exoplanetary science. To enhance event detection, we've developed a new method that utilizes a machine learning algorithm based on planetary transits. This approach trains on a dataset of known planetary systems and their characteristic features to identify new occurrences. By testing the method on simulated data, we've demonstrated its effectiveness in reproducing known results and accurately estimating the mass ratios of two-particle systems. Notably, our results indicate that the method can recover events with smaller mass ratios than previous techniques. We anticipate that this method will significantly contribute to the analysis of future Kepler data releases. Furthermore, we've discovered that the method can be adapted to identify multi-body phenomena and are exploring its potential to reveal signatures of gravitational scattering events. In probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, a structural assumption is often made about the underlying covariance matrix, yet estimating this matrix with uncertainty remains a challenging task. This paper addresses that issue by developing a new sparse covariance matrix estimator, based on the lasso regularization, that outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in large-scale settings. Theoretical and experimental evidence confirm that this estimator achieves optimal performance. Furthermore, a screening approach is introduced to reduce computational costs associated with lasso, and several methods are proposed to accurately predict origin-destination demands under the assumed structural framework. The efficacy of the proposed estimator and prediction methods is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on a real-world transportation dataset. The associated R code can be accessed via the repository https://github.com/asharafian/lasso_covariance.

Ultimately, we show that in one-dimensional cases with small values of λ, solutions derived using local energy estimates or entropy behave similarly to the self-similar self-repulsive entropy-regularizing solution. By combining the pre-training of speech and a secondary task such as phonotactic analysis or language modeling, we discover that a two-stage training method enhances the representation of speech utterances. The advantage is also more pronounced when the secondary task is phonotactic analysis rather than language modeling. The analysis suggests that the secondary task aids in learning more robust speech representations by reducing noise and filling gaps in the speech signal.  The improved representations, in turn, contribute to better recognition performance. Self-supervised learning has gained significant attention in the area of session-based recommendation. By leveraging large amounts of interaction data to train encoders and learn session representations, self-supervised learning enhances data augmentation capabilities. However, existing methods have limitations, such as relying on session representation similarity to group similar sessions together. This approach is not always effective, as it relies on negative samples that do not contribute much to the learning process. To address this, we introduce a novel method that combines self-supervised learning with a contrastive loss augmented by informative negative samples. We propose to select these samples based on their proximity to the target session, outperforming previous methods that rely on random negative choices. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over current session-based recommendation systems. The source code can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuyang1997/CSS.OLG.

Researchers have successfully integrated transition metal atoms into a silicon crystal structure using a Kingdon evaporation source, achieving a temperature range of 450-550 C.  Variations of the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in silicon are highly dependent on the placement of the dopants.  To create an array of reliable quantum processors, specifically two-qubit gates, precise placement of these dopants is crucial.  A statistical model was developed to analyze the dopant placement accuracy provided by the Kingdon source, which indicated a standard deviation of placement of 5.4 nm.  This was achieved through the examination of cross-sectional images taken with a transmission electron microscope.  The findings of this study demonstrate the potential for the use of the Kingdon source in the creation of robust and efficient silicon-based quantum processors.  A standard deviation of 5.4 nm is comparable to current state-of-the-art implantation techniques, which have a standard deviation of 1 nm.  However, the use of the Kingdon source has the added benefit of being able to create complex three-dimensional structures, which could lead to improved performance in quantum computing.  A study of the growth parameters showed that temperature has a significant impact on placement accuracy, with higher temperatures resulting in a larger standard deviation of placement.  A statistical analysis of the dopant placement revealed that the shape of the droplets created by the Kingdon source is key to achieving accurate placement, with spherical droplets resulting in a more uniform distribution of the dopants.  A model was also developed to analyze the impact of gravity on the dopant placement, which resulted in a standard deviation of placement of 7.8 nm when considering a flat surface, but only 4.8 nm when considering a perfectly spherical surface.  This study provides a deeper understanding of the physics behind the Kingdon source and its potential applications in the creation of silicon-based quantum processors.  A future study could involve analyzing the impact of the Kingdon source on the creation of monolithic three-dimensional silicon quantum processors.  A potential application of this research is the creation of a 20-qubit quantum processor using the Kingdon source.  A study of the scalability of the process revealed that the use of the Kingdon source is feasible for the creation of large-scale silicon-based quantum processors.  A potential future study could involve analyzing the impact of the Kingdon source on the creation of III-V semiconductor quantum processors.  A potential application of this research is the creation of a 50-qubit quantum processor using the Kingdon source.

Let's consider a projective variety of type X_n, defined as the intersection of n hypersurfaces in projective space, each of degree two in a hyperplane. We've developed a method to calculate the transitivity degree for these varieties and applied it to specific cases, such as varieties of type Segre embedding of Grassmannians and maximal links of singularities. Additionally, we've established a formula for the transitivity degree of a general type X_n and derived explicit values for certain varieties, including those of type G_2 and T_1. The proof relies on the study of 1-cycles in line bundles associated with these varieties, using a combination of methods from effective divisors, vanishing theorems, and the use of specific sections to represent 1-cycles. Furthermore, we've computed the transitivity degree for some varieties of type T_2 and provided a general approach for computing the transitivity degree in specific cases. The findings are illustrated with examples, including a variety of type T_2 in dimension 11. The obtained transitivity degrees are now available in the LMFDB database under the heading "Transitive embeddings". The accompanying GitHub repository includes code to verify these values. We present a numerical model for simulating charge carrier generation in photonic devices that utilize two-photon absorption. The carrier generation is modeled by solving a continuity equation for each charge carrier type, taking into account their respective drift and diffusion movements, assisted by a device-specific mesh system. For accurate simulation, we break down the carrier generation process into distinct time steps, combining it with the drift-diffusion model, which we solve using a transfinite interpolation method within each time step. To further enhance precision, we employ an implicit scheme for solving the time-dependent continuity equations. The mesh system allows for the device structure and semiconductor properties to be defined with a high degree of accuracy. The model has been successfully validated by comparing its results with those obtained from a commercial tool, specifically two-photon absorption simulations. The study demonstrates the model's capability to accurately simulate charge carrier dynamics in silicon materials, which is essential for the development of two-photon programmable photonic devices. The model has been implemented in a publicly available Python tool, which is described in the accompanying documentation. In this research, we examine the trade-offs inherent in the dynamics model learned through deep reinforcement. A significant challenge in this area is the presence of spurious dynamics, generated by chance, which can cause controllers to malfunction. Our investigation reveals that constraining the likelihood noise in the dynamics model to be below a certain threshold has an unexpected effect - it can make the controllers more prone to failure. This finding is rationalized by the observation that the spurious dynamics can act as a bridge, enabling the learned controller to reach target states that are not reachable through the real dynamics. To address this issue, we propose a method that utilizes the diversity of models to eliminate spurious dynamics. This method is based on the principle that spurious dynamics typically exhibit irregular behavior when multiple models are available. Our results show that this method outperforms existing approaches in eliminating spurious dynamics and enhancing robustness. This paper presents an NLP case study that aims to tackle the diverse issues of language, including the ambiguity of communication, by drawing on concepts from epistemology. The proposed method, based on the principles of epistemological social constructivism, involves a series of reasoning steps that mimic the thought process of an idealized, omniscient being. The Wikipedia knowledge base is utilized to implement these reasoning strategies, and the results are demonstrated in a Python environment. The paper's findings are presented in terms of achieved precision levels. The presented work is a theoretical framework for NLP that aspires to promote socially responsible AI development. It also presents a strategy for applying this method to the xG4 algorithm, resulting in a significantly improved version. Furthermore, the method is applied to F5 and xF5, leading to enhanced versions of these algorithms as well. The paper includes a detailed implementation of the new methods in the Singular package GröbSols. This package provides a framework for computing Gröbner bases using signatures and has been successfully used in solving various practical problems. The computational results demonstrate the algorithms' efficiency and effectiveness. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for rendering line joins in vector graphics, specifically for fan-shaped connections like notches and arrowheads. The traditional "sub-path" method is limited in producing smooth, continuous fan shapes, so we've developed a new approach using a continuous B-spline surface that accurately represents the desired fan-shaped line joins. The proposed algorithm directly utilizes B-spline curves and surfaces, bypassing discrete sampling, to significantly reduce rendering artifacts and improve performance. Comprehensive tests demonstrate the superior results obtained with this new algorithm over traditional methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework facilitates the creation of high-quality anti-aliasing for arrowheads and other notch-based shapes, enabling seamless and efficient rendering of line segments with such features. The algorithm has been successfully integrated into the Firefox browser, leading to a noticeable enhancement in rendering quality. The accompanying video showcases the differences in rendering quality using various techniques. The complete implementation is available on GitHub: https://github.com/mozilla/bq/tree/bspline-joins. Pulsar halos, formed by the decay of neutral pion secondaries from the bow shock nebulae of old pulsars, may hold the key to resolving the long-standing enigmas of the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess. A statistical study of pulsar radiation components across the entire electromagnetic spectrum is crucial for this purpose. To date, a comprehensive statistical analysis of pulsar gamma-ray emission has been conducted using the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope data for 165 pulsars. However, a similar study for optical pulsars has yet to be undertaken. This work presents a statistical investigation of the optical light curves of 85 pulsars using the SuperWASP data, employing a Bayesian approach to characterize the population distribution of pulsar spin periods, magnetic fields, and inclination angles. The results are then utilized to develop a model for pulsar optical emission, enabling the calculation of the total optical photon luminosity of the pulsar population. This, in turn, allows for the calculation of the optical photons produced by pulsar halos, ultimately contributing to the diffuse optical background. The findings of this study can be employed to investigate the optical component of the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess through Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, the results can be applied to examine the optical emission from pulsar halos in relation to the cosmic positron excess. The research presented here lays the groundwork for a comprehensive statistical analysis of pulsar emission across the entire optical spectrum, paving the way for a future study that will utilize the Gaia data to investigate pulsar spatial distribution. Deep learning models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks, have become
the gold standard for image classification. However, their reliance on extensive
image datasets and labor-intensive labeling makes them costly. We investigate
how Data Augmentation can be used to reduce the required number of training
images. Our approach focuses on generating masks to group image elements and
create augmented versions. By doing so, we enable the use of a smaller image
dataset. Our results show that using this method yields high accuracy when
compared to traditional Data Augmentation techniques. Additionally, we provide
code for reproducing our findings. 

Our approach consists of two main components:
1. A custom mask creation technique based on super-pixel clustering that
identifies relevant image features and generates masks automatically.
2. An evaluation of the impact of varying mask sizes on Convolutional Neural
Network performance.

We applied our method to the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with a ResNet-18
architecture and observed a significant reduction in the number of training
images required for achieving high accuracy classification results. 

Our method offers several benefits:
- It eliminates the need for manually designing augmentation strategies.
- It allows for the creation of diverse augmented versions from a limited
image set.
- It facilitates the use of existing pre-trained models without the need
for retraining on modified datasets. 

Our results indicate that using our method yields high accuracy when compared to
traditional Data Augmentation techniques, while also allowing for a substantial
reduction in the number of training images required.

The success of a dialogue system in natural conversations is heavily influenced by its role specifications, which outline expected conversational behaviors. However, crafting these role specifications is a complex and time-consuming task, requiring significant expertise. This paper proposes a data-driven method to automate this process by identifying relevant role specifications from annotated dialogue datasets. The approach leverages a pre-trained language model to create dialogue context representations and a contrastive learning technique to determine effective role specifications. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method, achieving comparable performance on standardized role specification-driven dialogue benchmarks with models trained on annotated data, and outperforming existing unsupervised role specification extraction methods. Furthermore, the method's applicability is showcased through successful applications in two challenging scenarios. The source code for this method is publicly available.

Additionally, we provide abductive evidence for the importance of attention networks in item ranking. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and dataset are publicly available.

Wikipedia editors who make changes can serve as labelers, helping to improve sentence quality ratings by identifying problematic sentences. This approach surpasses traditional data labeling techniques by leveraging the collective wisdom of all editors' actions, effectively treating them as a series of inferring labels. We evaluate this method on a dataset of Wikipedia articles and find that it yields comparable results to human labelers and outperforms automated labelers. Notably, this method can also provide insights into what changes editors make and why, offering insight into their decision processes. By utilizing the vast amount of data from Wikipedia edits, we can create a labeling method that is both accurate and scalable. This method can be adapted to other tasks by analyzing the relationships between edited content and their corresponding labels. We make our code and dataset available for public use. Moreover, we present a theoretical framework for inferring labels from edits, which can be applied to other tasks by analyzing the relationships between edited content and their corresponding labels. DB3 acquires knowledge by making inquiries and receiving feedback on its decision-making processes, distinguishing it from traditional methods that rely on training data. Calibrating the end-effector of a robotic arm can be a complex task. Typically, intrinsic parameters of the end-effector are assumed to be known, but this assumption is not valid when using a generic end-effector. Our proposed method utilizes a depth camera to enhance the precision of end-effector pose estimation during calibration. By doing so, we leverage the combination of visual and depth data to improve robustness, particularly in challenging scenarios with low light or distant targets. Our method framework is comprised of a pose estimation network that localizes the end-effector in relation to the camera, as well as a regression module that refines the estimated pose. Our results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing calibration techniques, achieving precise results in various environments. Our code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyizhao/end_effector_calibration.

Quantum computing has been gaining momentum, with quantum simulation becoming a crucial aspect. We've significantly improved the classical simulation of quantum circuits employing Clifford and T gates, a common quantum computing model, by T-offloading. This method involves replacing T gates with polynomial-sized expressions of geodesics in a non-Commutative 2D Euclidean space, enabling classical simulation with a linear increase in computational resources. Consequently, we've derived a corresponding upper limit on the approximate calculation of output probabilities in quantum computations, demonstrating that a polynomial number of geodesic expressions can accurately simulate the quantum circuit's output distribution to a high degree of precision. This achievement represents a significant advancement in classical simulation of circuits containing T gates, surpassing previous limits established by Aaronson and Kokainis, with a notable case study involving Shor's algorithm for integer factorization. Furthermore, we've successfully simulated circuits containing up to 14 qubits for 100 steps, a feat previously thought to be in the realm of quantum computing alone. This work has been made publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/alexhutch123/T-offloading. We've also developed a Python package, t_offloading, to facilitate the classical simulation of quantum circuits containing T gates. This package can be installed via pip using the command 'pip install t-offloading'. We've included a detailed usage guide in the package's documentation. Furthermore, we found that the optimal regularization level depends on the ratio of model complexity to data complexity. These insights are used to develop a new training approach, adaptive regularization, which adjusts the regularization level based on the observed loss curve and the specific epoch, ultimately leading to improved generalization performance. The method is then successfully applied to multiple challenging scenarios, including training overcomplete networks and from noisy data. The findings of this study also provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between model complexity and data properties. This research investigates the concept of dimension reduction for vectors in normed spaces. Specifically, it's about whether a given space can be mapped to a lower-dimensional space while preserving distances up to a certain error margin. While it has been observed that language models with higher perplexity tend to excel in in-context learning, the connection between language modeling performance (measured by perplexity) and few-shot learning performance (measured by accuracy) is not consistently guaranteed. Our approach significantly reduces the computational cost while maintaining similar planning quality in comparison to traditional methods. We test its effectiveness on various multi-limbed robots and showcase its ability to handle real-time constraints. Tight-binding models, specifically in their velocity form, face a significant drawback when attempting to predict electromagnetic responses. This limitation stems from the velocity gauge's inability to account for long-range dipole interactions, leading to inaccurate results. To address this issue, we introduce a corrective approach that can effectively mitigate these inaccuracies in velocity-based tight-binding models. By integrating dipole interactions through a cluster perturbation theory, we derive an improved electromagnetic response that applies to a range of systems. Our method is showcased with calculations on a two-dimensional semiconductor system, where the predictions align well with quantum Monte Carlo simulations. This approach offers a practical solution for enhancing the accuracy of velocity-based tight-binding models. Moreover, it provides a framework for first-principles modeling of quantum systems with strong electronic correlations. The method can be extended to higher-dimensional systems and may also be applicable to other models beyond the tight-binding framework. The code used for these calculations is available online at https://git.io/WeSTB.

The success of position tracking in motion control systems heavily relies on dynamics that are independent of position. However, systems that follow this criterion precisely are rare in practice. Often, systems that come close enough for practical purposes are modeled using a simplified constant coefficient approach, treating any position-dependent dynamics as insignificant. Yet, in many cases, neglecting these dynamics can lead to substantial performance losses. This paper presents a method to improve the effectiveness of an existing constant coefficient controller by accounting for the system's position-dependent dynamics. The improvement is achieved through a memory-based approach that uses past and present measurement history to compensate for the errors caused by simplification. The controller's modified design is then tested on a real-world system, with the results showing a significant performance boost compared to the traditional constant coefficient method. Furthermore, the designed controller outperforms a system model-based approach, with the tested outcome validating the proposed method's applicability to real-world scenarios. The presented research is relevant to the field of motion control and contributes to the development of more accurate predictive models. Additionally, the presented controller is a viable option for practical use. The research is also accompanied by a video showcasing the experimental results' time-series progression. Self-supervised point cloud learning networks can effectively extract features from 3D data, but their learned representations are often specific to the task of point cloud registration. This study investigates the potential of these features in object classification tasks. This involves combining the features with a novel contrastive loss to maximize the similarity between point clouds of the same object and minimize it between point clouds of different objects. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on three datasets, resulting in performance superior to other self-supervised methods. Action anticipation, a crucial aspect of machine vision, enables systems to project future actions from unlabeled video sequences. Current action anticipation models typically employ a straightforward approach, predicting future actions as a collective of basic actions. However, this method is limited in its ability to capture complex, high-level semantic information about future actions. To address this limitation, we present a novel approach called Action Semantic RBF, which utilizes semantically rich kernel representations to project future actions. By incorporating Radial Basis Function kernels that mirror action semantics, our method effectively captures high-level semantic information about future actions. We further enhance our approach by introducing a kernel learning module that automatically discovers the most relevant action semantics. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art action anticipation models on three benchmark datasets, as shown in our experimental results. We've analyzed data from the Mini-Megstar stellar simulator experiment to gain insights into the effects of its filters on observations of M dwarfs experiencing flares. The experiment involved imaging M dwarfs with the Mini-Megstar's optical and far ultraviolet filters while it was set up to mimic the conditions of the high-energy astrophysical environment. The observed spectra with the optical filter revealed broadened hydrogen lines that changed in response to changes in the optical and far ultraviolet brightness. The observed line behavior is consistent with the idea that high-energy photons from the flare are scattering off free electrons in the chromosphere, causing the line broadening. The line broadening also showed a correlation with the far ultraviolet emission, suggesting that the line formation region is located where the UV emission originates. The findings of this study have implications for the interpretation of data from future missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission. The results also highlight the potential of using the line broadening as an indicator of high-energy flares in low-mass stars. The study's data and analysis methods are available for public use. Compared to existing methods, the proposed solution significantly enhances certified accuracy in the presence of twisting deformations for 3D object recognition. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of a Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar network's interference effects. By developing a mathematical model, we quantify the interference that a specific radar connection experiences due to other FMCW radar connections sharing the same bandwidth. The model allows us to determine the probability of interference that a particular radar connection may encounter. The FMCW radar system's properties, such as the number of chirps per packet and the system's resolution, significantly influence these interference probabilities. The accuracy of our mathematical model is verified through simulations. Based on the interference probabilities, we design a Throughput-Oriented Chirp Allocation (TOCA) protocol that assigns chirp packets to each radar connection. The TOCA protocol dynamically schedules FMCW radar connections to minimize interference and maximize overall system throughput. The efficacy of the TOCA protocol is demonstrated through comparative simulations with Random Chirp Allocation (RCA) and Fixed Chirp Allocation (FCA) methods. The TOCA protocol outperforms RCA and FCA in terms of system throughput while maintaining high success rates for high-priority connections. The TOCA protocol also offers a trade-off between throughput and interference success rates for various system configurations. The TOCA protocol's parameters can be adjusted to accommodate different QoS requirements. The TOCA protocol's design is versatile and can be applied to various FMCW radar configurations. Temporal knowledge graph completion involves determining missing relationships in knowledge graphs over time. Current approaches enhance traditional knowledge graph embedding techniques with time information, yet neglect cycle patterns in time encodings. To address this, we introduce a novel time-encoding method that considers both forward and backward timeline cycles. This cycle-aware approach involves time-point embedding based on temporal relations and aggregates them into time-encoding vectors using the maximum principle. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our cycle-aware time-encoding scheme, achieving state-of-the-art results on several temporal knowledge graph completion datasets. A common issue with recommender systems is the data sparsity problem, where users' preferences for items are unknown. To address this challenge, we explore the effectiveness of document modeling-based methods in handling sparse data. These methods utilize a global model to capture item representations and have shown promise in natural language processing tasks. However, their application in recommender systems is limited. The method employs a novel loss function that combines cross-entropy loss with a constraint to ensure the generated latent space is semantically preserved. Experimental results demonstrate the method's efficacy in handling sparse data and its ability to outperform existing techniques in several recommender system datasets. Machine learning systems face a significant challenge in balancing performance and fairness. In this study, we explore how certain techniques can be combined to achieve Fairness through the Absence of a Selected Variable (FASV), ensuring no bias is introduced by the model. We specifically examine the effect of using multiple fairness metrics, variations of federated learning, and different applications of differential privacy. Our findings are based on an extensive experiment involving 19 datasets and 4 metrics, revealing that employing various fairness metrics leads to inconsistent and unfair models, despite the implementation of differential privacy. This highlights the need for a systematic approach to developing machine learning systems that prioritize FASV. To aid researchers, we introduce a framework that automates the process of selecting suitable combinations of fairness metrics, federated learning configurations, and differential privacy settings. This framework is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/alexandria-ai/fasv. Our results show that a specific combination of metrics and differential privacy outperforms other options in achieving FASV. Furthermore, we introduce a novel concept called fairness loss drift, which enables early detection of bias in the model. This drift metric can be applied in various contexts, including both centralized and federated learning settings. Our research demonstrates the importance of carefully designing the machine learning pipeline to ensure the absence of bias. To this end, we propose a new approach called Pipeline Fairness Analysis, which enables the identification of fairness issues at different stages of the pipeline. This approach can be used to automatically select the most effective combinations of techniques in achieving FASV. Our experiments reveal that the fairness of the model is often compromised by the data selection process in federated learning. This highlights the need for a more transparent and fair data sharing policy. These states were discovered in the $J/\psi K^+$ decay channel using data collected by the LHCb detector in proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV. The $B_c^*$ decay distributions were fitted to determine the states' masses and decay width, yielding a mass of 6485.12 $\pm$ 0.29 (stat.) $\pm$ 0.25 (syst.) MeV for $B_c^*(6830)^+$ and 7073.3 $\pm$ 1.0 (stat.) $\pm$ 1.5 (syst.) MeV for $B_c^*(7075)^+$. The observed states were determined to have the quantum numbers $J/P = 1^1$ and $2^1$ respectively. Convolutional and recurrent neural networks are fundamental components of deep learning, used extensively in signal and image processing. When fine-tuning pre-trained networks, updating all weights can be inefficient, especially with convolutional layers. We introduce local critic training, a method where only weights in the immediate forward path are updated during backpropagation, significantly improving efficiency. Local critic training is a general technique, applicable to recurrent, transposed, and self-attention layers, and is particularly beneficial for convolutional layers in computer vision. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness in reducing training time by up to 2 times, with comparable performance, and make the source code available.

This study explores the impact of dissipation that is extremely low but sufficient to cause a significant change in behavior. In particular, it examines how very weak dissipation affects the transition from smooth, boundary-changing transitions to more complex, interior transformations in chaotic scattering. The latter type of change typically occurs when dissipation levels are much lower than what is commonly studied. Theoretical and numerical analyses conducted in this research reveal that very weak dissipation can indeed lead to complex, interior changes in a system known as the standard map's triple well. However, these findings are also influenced by a numerical error that arises from the use of a fixed point iteration method to solve the system's equations. The error is significant when dissipation levels are as low as $10^{-9}$ and can even cause the system to exhibit patterns that resemble those associated with more powerful dissipation levels. The accuracy of the numerical results was verified by analyzing the statistical properties of the system at large scales. The research also presents a method to correct for the error in question, which is particularly relevant in situations where very low dissipation levels are necessary but not easily replicated in numerical simulations. This paper introduces a Spatial-Temporal Attention network, specifically designed for Global Local Attention network (GAN), to focus on key video frame areas and efficient motion information. The spatial attention mechanism employs a multi-stage approach to filter out less important areas, selecting more relevant ones to maintain. To extract efficient motion information, the temporal attention mechanism is applied to diminish noise in motion patterns. This results in a more compact and effective motion feature representation. The combination of these mechanisms enables the model to gain in-depth understanding of video content. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on action recognition tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhenghuihui/GANs.

This study develops a versatile computational method for estimating the entropy of a given probability distribution, even in cases where the distribution cannot be directly quantified. The method is based on an inverse problem that generates samples from a given, approximate entropy constraint. The entropy approximation is framed as a maximum principle, with the actual distribution represented as a limit of a sequence of distributions defined on discrete, high-dimensional spaces. The method is tested using various probability distributions, with results showing its effectiveness and accuracy. The associated code is freely available online. This paper introduces a dynamic occupancy model of continuous-time Borel measures, which represents key characteristics of semiconductor production systems. It demonstrates how this measure model can be utilized in various applications, including calculating initial states and exit rates for systems modeled with jump processes. A special case of this model, discrete measure modeling with jump processes, has been previously studied. Our approach generalizes this discrete model to a continuous form, which is particularly beneficial for applications with infinite state spaces. A primary example is used to illustrate the method's effectiveness. It calculates the probability of a measure representing a production line in a specific state after a given time, as well as the rate at which production lines exit a specified state. These calculations are essential for evaluating performance metrics in order to optimize semiconductor manufacturing systems. Our approach also includes a comparison of the rate of change for measures representing systems modeled with different types of processes, including continuous, semi-continuous, and jump processes. These comparisons are essential for selecting the most suitable model for a given application. To safeguard IoT systems from cyber threats, it is crucial to have attack classifiers that can run in real-time directly on devices. However, current attack classifiers often require significant computational power, making them unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained IoT devices. To address this issue, we have developed a tool called NBcoded, which converts neural network-based attack classifiers into a form that can be implemented using n-gram Bayesian classifiers, thus allowing them on devices with limited resources. NBcoded achieves this conversion by analyzing the neural network's weights and translating them into conditional probability tables, and it supports various network architectures, including fully connected and convolutional types. Experimental results show that NBcoded accurately recreates the original neural network classifications on IoT devices, and it outperforms other conversion methods in terms of accuracy. Additionally, NBcoded provides a significant computational speedup, allowing it to run up to 20 times faster on devices like the Raspberry Pi 3. The NBcoded tool is now available for public use. \end{abstract}

We've derived finite presentation representations for specific class groups of number fields, and this work generalizes to certain classes of groups, including metabelian groups, where the representation complexity is determined by a parameter linked to group properties. The representation size grows at a polynomial rate, influenced by the group's properties, like being finitely presented or torsion-free. Notably, the growth gap differs significantly between these properties. Additionally, our findings apply to the ambient general linear groups, and the results are contrasted with the maximal solvable subgroups of general linear groups. The proof involves combining tools from number theory, group theory, and computational complexity, particularly Ehrenfeut's finiteness theorem and the Boguslawski-Feferman complexity bound. The work also includes a study of the representation complexity of nilpotent groups, specifically those of steps two or higher, where the findings are more nuanced and influenced by group invariants. The representations are computationally efficient, running within polynomial time bounds, and the work concludes by exploring open questions and potential directions for further research. This study investigates the feasibility of hybrid quantum approaches for solving complex optimization issues within power grid analysis. Specifically, we examine the hybridization of quantum and classical methods for the minimum feedback set problem in cycle-free graphs, which is a critical problem in power network partitioning. Our research demonstrates that hybrid quantum solutions can outperform classical methods, particularly for smaller-sized instances, while also highlighting the importance of selecting suitable problem sizes for hybridization. The study also showcases two distinct hybrid quantum approaches: one using a quantum algorithm combined with a classical heuristic, and the other employing a mixed quantum-classical algorithm. The experiments were conducted on a superconducting quantum processor and a simulator of a quantum approximate digital processor. The results indicate that for smaller circuits of around 100-400 edges, the hybrid approach can achieve a speedup of up to three orders of magnitude compared to classical methods. We've developed a soft potential model to describe the interaction between high-frequency acoustic waves and low-frequency electrostatic plasma oscillations in metals. By applying the model to Al, Cu, and Hg, we've successfully reproduced the observed damping patterns of longitudinal sound waves. Notably, the model predicts a specific behavior at low frequencies, indicating a particular damping characteristic. Interestingly, this prediction aligns with recent experiments conducted by Giannozzi et al. (Nature Communications 2019), providing further validation of the model's accuracy. Additionally, we've used the model to estimate the strength of long-range intermetallic forces, yielding values consistent with existing estimates for Al and mercury, but significantly higher for copper. This model offers a new approach to studying the physics of long-range forces in metals. (c) 2023 The Authors. Published by IOP Publishing Ltd. and British Institute of Physics. All rights reserved.

We introduce a semi-numerical method that iteratively refines analytical equations by incorporating numerical data, allowing for breakthroughs in high-precision predictions in particle physics. By combining this approach with differential equations, we can generate analytical solutions that are subsequently numerically enhanced for even more accurate results. This novel methodology is initially demonstrated in a straightforward calculation, before being applied to a complex problem in QCD to a remarkable degree of precision (around one part in ten thousand). This technique is anticipated to significantly contribute to future particle physics experiments. Furthermore, the underlying framework has a broad range of applications and can be adapted to various fields of study. We introduce a novel approach to identify and utilize non-diffracting eigenchannels
in wave propagation. By leveraging the scattering matrix, which summarizes a system's properties,
we compute eigenchannels and corresponding eigenvalues experimentally. These eigenchannels
are shown to correspond directly with the intensity patterns of waves within the system,
enabling their identification and characterization in real-time. This method is applied in a non-diffracting
diffraction pattern analyzer, allowing us to isolate non-diffracting eigenchannels and reconstruct
their spatial patterns. This reconstruction method provides a framework for understanding and utilizing
the transmission properties of lasers and other coherent light sources. Additionally, we demonstrate
the feasibility of utilizing these eigenchannels for enhancing the depth of focus of a Gaussian beam. 
This approach offers a general and applicable method for analyzing the transmission properties of various systems. 
This technique is expected to contribute to the development of improved laser-based technologies.

This paper explores the stable matching problem, specifically computing an exact stable matching that maximizes utilitarian welfare. We investigate this problem under various valuation models when agents have limited preference options. For binary valuations, this problem falls under the P-complete class, but we found it to be NP-complete when constraints are applied to the number of acceptable options. When agents can rank a limited number of options, we established NP-completeness results. These findings provide a comprehensive complexity analysis, addressing an open question in the field. Furthermore, we introduced a heuristic approach based on the local search method and analyzed its approximation ratio and running time complexity. Interestingly, this problem becomes more complex when preferences are constrained to the left or right, yielding P-complete and NP-complete results for binary and general valuations, respectively. Lastly, we examined the parameterized complexity of the exact stable matching problem and found fixed-parameter tractable solutions for some parameters, but others led to parameterized P-complete results. Our work also introduced a new fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for the fuzzy stable matching problem. These findings significantly expand the existing literature on parameterized complexity for stable matching problems. Our proposed heuristic approach is evaluated through experiments using synthetic data, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness. These findings are further validated by empirical analysis of real-world data. Our code is available online for replication purposes. To our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the parameterized complexity of exact stable matching problems. These findings are expected to contribute to the development of more efficient algorithms for exact stable matching problems. Our code is available online for replication purposes. Quantum error correction is a critical area of research, particularly so since several decoding methods struggle with diverse noise scenarios. To address this, we employ reinforcement learning in a quantum error correcting code to develop a more effective decoding strategy. Specifically, we utilize a quantum reinforcement learning model that combines a quantum neural network policy with a quantum value function, both of which are trained in a quantum environment that simulates the effects of noise. Our results indicate that this approach yields a higher fidelity than standard belief propagation in diverse noise conditions. Furthermore, we find that the quantum reinforcement learning method excels in scenarios where the noise pattern changes over time. To facilitate the training of these complex quantum models, we introduce a method that simplifies the process. Our code is available at https://github.com/Cheng-CMU/Quantum-Reinforcement-Learning-for_DEC.

Our research uses the parton-hadron transport model (PHEN) to simulate Au+Au collisions at 2.76 AGeV and examine the momentum distribution of final-state hadrons. In the transport model, we introduce an additional interaction coefficient, $\lambda_{\pi N}$, which influences the yield of produced pions. By adjusting this coefficient, we find that the yield of pions is highly sensitive to it. Furthermore, we investigate how the quark's momentum fraction, denoted as $x_Q$, affects the yield of hadrons. In Au+Au collisions, the yield of hadrons decreases as $x_Q$ decreases. Additionally, we observe that the spectral shape of protons exhibits a mass dependence and in central Au+Au collisions, the yield of hadrons is significantly lower than in Pb+Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. Lastly, we examine the anisotropic flow of hadrons and find that the elliptical flow, $v_2$, and triangular flow, $v_3$, are both sensitive to the quark's momentum fraction, $x_Q$. In Au+Au collisions, the flow coefficients increase as $x_Q$ decreases. Conversely, the yield of hadrons decreases as $x_Q$ decreases. representations are easily interpretable, making it a valuable tool for data

We've enhanced the computational efficiency of flow simulations that feature floating objects by adapting a multi-timestep approach originally designed for solid boundaries. This innovation allows us to directly incorporate forces acting on boundaries into the numerical scheme, eliminating the need for artificial cross-boundary influences and related stability constraints typically associated with previous methods. As a result, we've successfully eliminated the artificial CFL condition that typically limited our simulation's temporal resolution. We've also developed a system for automatically generating multi-timestep schemes for any given equation set, which we've applied to simulate a range of complex flows involving objects that interact with the surrounding fluid. Our results show that the new method outperforms traditional approaches while producing accurate results that align with experimental data and alternative simulation strategies. Additionally, we've derived a theoretical foundation for our multi-timestep scheme, which we've validated through a series of numerical tests. This new method offers a substantial temporal resolution boost – up to four times in our examples – without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, we've successfully simulated turbulent flows that feature objects with complex geometries and observed accurate vorticity dynamics around these boundaries. Our multi-timestep approach has the potential to significantly expand the range of applicable FICM simulations. We've made the necessary code publically available to facilitate future research. We examine the concept of particle number definition in relation to Hawking radiation and black hole horizons. It's demonstrated that different number definition methods lead to varying particle number counts during the black hole evaporation process. These results are then graphically represented to illustrate the methods. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings on the information paradox and the nature of black holes. Ultimately, we conclude that the choice of particle number definition is a matter of personal preference. Additionally, we touch on conservative methods for defining number operators and apply one such method to the model of black holes described by the Klein-Gordon equation. This yields a consistent particle number count of zero throughout the evaporation process. We also explore the possibility of extending this conservative method to the electromagnetic field, but find it yields a particle number count that does not align with Hawking's theory. However, we note that the Klein-Gordon model is not the only model that can resolve the information paradox in a consistent manner. Lastly, we outline the general form of number definition methods for any given field and potential energy barriers. This research investigates the dynamic behavior of a liquid jet that experiences cross-flow in a channel, focusing on how the surrounding air influences the shear jet boundary. An advanced numerical model is employed to simulate the two-phase flow and compare it with an earlier single-phase liquid model. The results show that the presence of entrained air significantly impacts the dynamic behavior of the jet, particularly in the shear layer and ligament formation regions. The single-phase model overestimates the growth rates of perturbations and ligament lengths when air is not accounted for. However, the two-phase model reveals that ligaments can only sustain themselves if they contain a certain percentage of air. This finding has implications for understanding the dynamics of liquid metal jets in gas-phase environments. Furthermore, the study suggests that liquid metal jets can maintain their structure and travel long distances without breaking up, provided they contain a certain percentage of gas. This knowledge can inform strategies for designing stable liquid metal jets. Ultimately, the two-phase model provides a more accurate representation of jet dynamics and is essential for understanding and predicting various phenomena in liquid metal jets. The study also highlights the importance of considering the interactions between phases in numerical models of liquid metal jets. To assess the effectiveness of relational machine learning models in pharmacology, 
we conducted a comprehensive study comparing in silico binding affinity predictions 
for over 3000 drug-target pairs across diverse dimer and monomer targets. 
Our analysis considered various relational machine learning methods and their non-relational counterparts. 
The results revealed that relational models outperform non-relational models, 
yielding a 0.14 log unit improvement in binding affinity prediction accuracy. 
However, our findings also highlight the need for caution when selecting evaluation metrics 
and data representation to accurately capture the benefits of relational learning. 
Ultimately, this study provides guidance on evaluating pharmacological relational machine learning models.

The results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in accurately assessing road conditions in limited datasets. Furthermore, the approach provides actionable insights, which can be scaled up for larger projects. The code and data used in this research are freely available for public use. Imitation learning relies on a supervisor's domain knowledge, typically acquired through years of experience. Transferring this expertise to a machine learning agent's perspective can result in several challenges. This research explores the issue of environmental discrepancies between the supervisor's and agent's viewpoints, focusing on a specific case where the supervisor and agent have different reference frames. A novel approach is introduced to establish a common coordinate system by learning supervision from multiple experts. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful applications in two complex simulations: a Bimanual Reach and Grab task and a Kitchen Pouring Task. Establishing a unified agent-supervisor environment is crucial for effective imitation learning, ultimately enabling agents to acquire essential skills. Our approach provides a framework for achieving this goal. Additionally, our method has the added benefit of improving expert supervision for real-world applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexeydyatkov/frameless_imitation. A video showcasing our results can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q8Q8Q8Q8Q.

The process of protostar formation is a critical phase in the birth of stars. It occurs when a collapsing core breaks free from a larger cloud of gas. This process is often studied through numerical simulations, but the results are typically difficult to interpret due to the complex nature of the simulations. To gain more insight, we conducted a set of simulations in a controlled environment, focusing on the effects of angular momentum on the clouds. We found that clouds with high angular momentum tend to fragment their gases into multiple disks, rather than forming a single disk. This, in turn, affects the formation of protostars, as those in high angular momentum clouds tend to receive more material from their surrounding gases. Our results suggest that the mass of material accreted onto a protostar is directly related to the cloud's angular momentum. This relationship has significant implications for the formation of planetary systems, as high angular momentum clouds may produce multiple snow-line evolutions, leading to diverse and complex system architectures. Conversely, clouds with low angular momentum tend to form single-disk systems, free from fragmentation and potentially producing more uniform planetary systems. Our findings suggest that the angular momentum of a gas cloud plays a crucial role in determining the properties of a protostar and its surrounding disk system. This, in turn, affects the ultimate architecture of a planetary system. To further explore these effects, we plan to conduct additional simulations, varying the mass of the clouds and their magnetic fields to observe their impact on the formation of protostars and disks. These studies will provide a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in star and planetary system formation. reducing impact than incarceration in the long term.

interventions by prioritizing specific treatments for particular crimes and offenders.

Anomalous data detection is crucial in various applications. Traditional methods rely on manually labeled data, which can be time-consuming and impractical to obtain. This research addresses this challenge by identifying anomalous data without the need for labeled data. A new approach is proposed, combining unsupervised learning techniques to recognize patterns in normal data and detect abnormalities. The method utilizes a two-stage process: first, it identifies key features from the data using PCA; then, it classifies anomalies by clustering data points with low reconstruction errors. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets. The results show that this method outperforms standard techniques, specifically nearest neighbor and local outlier factor, in accurately identifying anomalous data. Furthermore, this method can be used to detect anomalies in real-time, making it suitable for applications with streaming data. The research includes a computational efficiency analysis, showing that this approach is scalable for large datasets. The method was implemented in Python and made available on GitHub for further evaluation by the research community. The proposed technique provides a reliable and efficient alternative to detecting anomalies in data. The code is accessible at the following URL: https://github.com/asharif2/AnomalyDetection. This study examines the performance of multiple verification systems in 
industrial settings, both with and without noise. We compare their output 
using metrics such as precision, recall, F1 score, and number of parts 
successfully identified. Notably, the ranking of verification systems 
changes depending on whether data is pristine or contains errors. To 
better understand their performance in realistic, noisy environments, 
we introduce a method for generating datasets that mimic industrial 
conditions. These datasets are based on actual data and replicate 
various types of errors commonly encountered in the field. We also 
investigate how adjusting the level of noise affects verification 
system output and how it compares to results from clean data. 
Conversely, we identify verification systems that excel in noisy 
conditions but struggle with clean data. Ultimately, this research 
highlights the necessity for testing verification systems across a 
range of data quality levels to ensure they can adapt to real-world 
scenarios. Additionally, our work provides a framework for creating 
datasets that accurately model industrial conditions, potentially 
enabling the development of more effective verification systems. 
Furthermore, our study's findings can inform the design of future 
verification systems, highlighting areas for improvement. 
Consequently, these contributions can lead to improved verification 
systems capable of handling the variety of errors encountered in 
industrial settings.

This study examines the effectiveness of data augmentation strategies for pre-trained models, specifically those utilizing BERT architecture. Our analysis covers diverse methods, including modifying input text, its alignment, and wondrous transformations, to what extent these strategies can be reduced to vector operations, and how they interact with other pre-processing components. By conducting a comprehensive set of experiments, we demonstrate that these enhancements yield substantial gains in limited-data scenarios but have a minimal impact when dealing with large amounts of training data. Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of pre-training data size, and we introduce a new efficient augmentation technique called TokenDrop. TokenDrop outperforms other methods in our evaluation and offers a 10x speed improvement over the best performing alternative. Moreover, we show that combining various data augmentation strategies can lead to overfitting on certain tasks, and we provide insights on how to integrate them safely. Our research and code are available at https://github.com/your-username/TokenDrop.

This result is crucial, as it enables us to establish the asymptotic normality of estimators for functions of parameters in regression models based on the generalized Blomqvist's ratio. Protecting sensitive data from unauthorized access is a critical concern in private data management systems. Existing research has primarily focused on individual data records, but overlooks the interdependence that exists between these records. In reality, data owners often utilize relationships between records to convey meaning, which can reveal sensitive information if not adequately protected. This paper introduces a new concept for record interdependence-based privacy protection, which can be achieved through a technique called Conditional Homomorphic Encryption. A practical implementation of this concept is also demonstrated using the BSW09 scheme. Additionally, the paper includes an empirical analysis of the performance of this implementation, utilizing real-world data from the Insurance Tableau. The results show that CHET can effectively safeguard record interdependence and prevent the disclosure of sensitive information, while incurring a computationally tolerable cost compared to other encryption methods. In particular, the performance evaluation reveals that the CHET implementation offers a more efficient trade-off between privacy and computational cost than alternative approaches. In conclusion, the paper highlights the potential of Conditional HE as a viable solution for protecting record interdependence and promoting private data usage. To meet this demand, detecting outfit mismatches has become essential for providing users with quality feedback. Current approaches rely on pre-annotated datasets and focus on identifying individual garment mismatches. This paper presents a novel solution that leverages user-created outfits on social media for real-time mismatch detection. Experimental results show our model's ability to detect mismatches with high precision and recall, especially when combined with traditional machine learning methods. This technology can be integrated into fashion apps to enhance user experience and provide quality feedback. Federated learning aims to merge local model updates from multiple devices with global aggregation, enabling distributed training while safeguarding data privacy. However, existing solutions have limitations due to large communication requirements, particularly when dealing with parameter sizes and gradient updates. To address this challenge, we present FedBuff, an efficient federated learning algorithm that significantly reduces communication needs. FedBuff achieves this through a combination of two techniques: gradient buffering and selective averaging. Gradient buffering temporarily stores gradient updates on each device, allowing for local aggregation and reduction of the communication burden during local epochs. Subsequently, selective averaging is employed on the aggregated gradients on the server-side to further minimize the data transfer during global aggregation. By incorporating an adaptive buffering strategy, FedBuff optimizes buffer usage and minimizes memory requirements. Our experimental results demonstrate that FedBuff outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in efficiency while maintaining data privacy. Notably, FedBuff exhibits enhanced robustness in high communication-cost settings and comparable performance in low communication-cost settings. Furthermore, our analysis shows that FedBuff converges at a rate comparable to existing algorithms. The source code for FedBuff is publicly available at https://github.com/alexalexandrov/FedBuff.

Recent findings suggest that primordial black holes (PBHs) could potentially account for all dark matter if they exist within a specific mass range, approximately $10^{14-22}$ grams. We have investigated the effects of a spatially varying dark matter potential on the motion of PBHs. These varying potentials, which could arise from certain cosmological models, result in an anisotropic force that impacts PBH motion. Consequently, we discovered that in such scenarios, PBHs cannot account for all dark matter, as their mean separation would be insufficient to explain its density. This anisotropic force may also lead to the clustering of PBHs, as their motion could result in the formation of networks of interconnected web-like structures. Furthermore, we found that PBHs with masses greater than $10^{18}$ grams would be gravitationally bound to the Galaxy's center, while those with lower masses would follow radial trajectories. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding PBH behavior in spatially inhomogeneous dark matter distributions. Additionally, we have explored the implications of a variable dark matter potential on the properties of cosmic strings and the motion of particles within the Galaxy. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of PBHs and their potential role in dark matter. Specifically, we have shown that even if cosmic strings are unstable, they would not decay into PBHs, as previously suggested. Our research also sheds light on the motion of particles within the Galaxy, as observed in the Kuzmin-Quevedo effect. We derive a formula to calculate the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set of a non-constant quasiregular self-map from the complex plane, excluding a small exceptional set. This formula aligns with a previous estimate by Baker and McMullen. Our method employs graph theory, particularly the concept of hyperbolic graphs, to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the Julia set and the set of infinite paths within a certain graph that exhibit escaping behavior. This correspondence enables accurate measurement of the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set. This dimension is also shown to be the same as that of the Julia set of a related holomorphic map, confirming a long-standing conjecture of Baker. Our approach is flexible and can be adapted to study other types of maps, such as those involving iterated function systems. Furthermore, we use graph theory to demonstrate that the Julia set of a quasiregular map is locally connected under specific conditions. Additionally, we explore the Julia sets of maps that are close to being holomorphic, revealing that they share many similarities with their holomorphic counterparts. This research also provides a new approach to studying the connectedness of Julia sets, offering potential applications and insights into related fields. This paper introduces SpecCon, a novel approach to unconditional audio generation that leverages a spectrogram-based loss function, enabling precise frequency manipulation. By pairing SpecCon with mode alignment, we develop a method for generating natural-sounding music without requiring labeled data. Our technique surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art Music Maestro system in the low-fidelity regime, while also producing high-quality outputs in the high-fidelity regime. Notably, our model exhibits superior capability in transferring style from one music piece to another, producing more realistic results in the process. Our implementation will be publicly available.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are commonly used for modeling sequential data but fully connected RNNs can be computationally expensive and challenging to train. Recent research has introduced sparse RNNs, reducing memory consumption and improving training efficiency by omitting unnecessary weight calculations. However, current methods rely on complex strategies involving multiple passes through the data and inefficient gradient computations. We present a new approach to sparsifying fully connected RNNs, eliminating zero gradients during backpropagation to accelerate training. Our method, inspired by the emerging vectorized operations on graphics processing units, enables simultaneous computation of vectorized gradients. The resulting model achieves a substantial reduction in memory usage and a 1.4-1.6 times speed increase over baseline RNNs, with comparable performance on benchmark datasets. Notably, our model outperforms existing sparse methods by 3-5% on the PTB dataset. The source code is available at https://github.com/alexeygush/sparnn.

Notably, our results indicate that timing and duration are critical factors influencing the outcome of these policies. This study provides evidence for policymakers on the potential of intermediate strategies to mitigate the pandemic's impact. Finally, our research demonstrates the utility of state-aggregated data in understanding the pandemic's dynamics and guiding policy decisions. Current data validation techniques rely on basic checks for individual data segments, but these approaches fall short in efficiently resolving complex issues and identifying data problems. To address this challenge, we introduce DataScope, an automated data debugging tool that rapidly locates and diagnoses problems within large datasets. DataScope operates by transforming each data transformation step in a pipeline into a query language, creating a logical graph representation that facilitates problem detection. By utilizing logical reasoning, DataScope can pinpoint data issues and provide meaningful, human-understandable explanations. Our experiments demonstrate that DataScope significantly outperforms traditional data validation methods, achieving a 2-3 fold improvement in processing time. Furthermore, DataScope's logical graph analysis enables the detection of problems that other methods cannot, showcasing its effectiveness in data debugging.
